claims.statement: The study comprises 786 children with JIA and 3908 matched controls in the primary study and 382 children with JIA and 1910 matched controls in the secondary study.

claims.statement: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis increases sickness school absence
claims.anchor_quote: Our primary study showed higher rates of sickness SA and total SA from 3 years before diagnosis and the following 5 years after diagnosis among children with JIA.

claims.intro_sentence: Similar trends with significant but decreasing IRR were seen when evaluating both sickness absence and legal absence rates in the years after diagnosis (Figure 1).
claims.scope_population: Children diagnosed with JIA after starting school (primary study), versus matched schoolmates without JIA

claims.notes: The total-absence IRRs for the primary study appear only in Figure 1; the extracted Figure 1 panel (dk_W4409457195::F1::A) contains a single row recording the matching ratio of JIA to control children, so no estimate of total school absence was extracted.

claims.intro_sentence: The aim of this study is therefore to assess and compare vaccination coverages at 6 weeks after scheduled vaccination and time to vaccination between a cohort of children vaccinated before and after the implementation of the proactive reminder system.

claims.statement: The article presents, as a contribution, an analytical model that brings private and public revenue streams together in a single model so that the transaction costs of the two sources can be compared.

claims.scope_population: nationwide voluntary social organisations
claims.scope_identification: analytical model combining private and public revenue streams

results.why: The female interaction in the quota-experiment earnings regression is the coefficient through which women's long-run earnings loss is identified. claims.notes: The abstract states nurses "could not be replaced on net despite public education ... expansion efforts"; the introduction states that education efforts were not effective in the short run, which supplies the explicit null direction.

results.why: The only extracted evidence on the education expansion: enrollment is a proxy for future nurse supply, and with a 4–5 year degree the modest 1994 increase cannot raise net nurse employment in the short run, so the sign cannot speak directly to the employment outcome. Derivation: New nurse enrollment 1994 [row 10] 2,515 − 1993 [row 9] 2,295 ≈ +220 students per year (+8.7%), which the text scales to 0.5% of nurse employment in hospitals and nursing homes, against a reform-induced loss of about 4,500 hospital nurses.

results.why: Counter-evidence to blanket representativeness: even after weighting, organic disorders remain substantially underrepresented. Derivation: Organic disorders weighted 0.30% [row 6] vs eligible 0.57% [row 4]: still ~47% below (Supplementary Table 4, p<0.001).

results.outcome_variable: (no axis title; categorical)

paper_metadata.title: Boys left behind: The effects of summer camp and follow-up strategies on academic, personal, and social competencies

claims.cause: summer camp participation combined with a one-year follow-up program
claims.notes: The abstract anchor announces positive effects on 'academic competencies' in general terms; the introduction names the concrete academic performance variable (average assessment mark) and its direction.

results.why: Entropy-balancing adjusted difference-in-differences event-study effect of camp/mentoring on the standardized average assessment mark at the first post-camp assessment — the estimate the author quotes as the 15% of a SD increase. Derivation: Entropy-balancing adjusted event-study estimate 0.16 SD at December grade 9, i.e. the 'around 15% of a standard deviation' stated in the introduction and the '15% of a standard deviation ... 6 ... months after' stated on p.5.
results.outcome_variable: Standardized effect size

results.why: Same quantity without the entropy-balancing reweighting (0.145 SD); the paper reports it alongside to show the covariate adjustment does not change the effect.
results.outcome_variable: Standardized effect size

results.why: Entropy-balancing adjusted event-study effect at the final grade 9 assessment, the 12-month horizon of the same claim, showing the gain persists to a year after the camp. Derivation: Entropy-balancing adjusted estimate 0.158 SD at June grade 9 ≈ the stated 'effects of 15% of a standard deviation both 6 and 12 months after camp/mentoring participation' (p.5).
results.outcome_variable: Standardized effect size

results.why: Unadjusted (raw difference-in-differences) version of the 12-month estimate, 0.151 SD.

results.why: Column (2) is the homogeneous-worker ACM specification that ignores human capital (and occupations); adjusting the printed C/ρ by the near-zero, wrong-signed 1/ρ gives switching costs several times the column (1) estimate, as the claim states. results.why: Baseline event study of first childbirth on earnings: women drop ~23 percent below their pre-birth path at event time 10 while men are unaffected, which is the ~20 percent long-run earnings gap the abstract states. Derivation: Female earnings coefficient at event time 10 [row 3] = −0.23 minus male earnings coefficient at event time 10 [row 4] = −0.03 gives a child-driven gender gap of about 0.20, i.e. the long-run child penalty of 0.194 printed in panel A (about 20 percent).
results.horizon: event time 10 (ten years after first birth)
results.outcome_variable: Earnings relative to t = −1

results.why: Very-long-run version of the same event study: the female earnings coefficient is still −0.21 at event time 20 against a male coefficient of 0, a distinct (20-year) horizon of the same earnings gap.
results.horizon: event time 20 (twenty years after first birth)
results.outcome_variable: Earnings relative to t = −1

results.why: Cohort-specific earnings penalties averaged over event times 0–10 sit on a flat line at about 25 percent, a positive child-driven earnings gap throughout the period covered by the claim.
results.horizon: average earnings penalty over event times 0–10, by birth cohort
results.outcome_variable: Average earnings penalty (%)

results.why: Same exercise at the 11–20 year horizon: the earliest plotted cohort shows an average earnings penalty of about 22 percent (declining to about 20 percent for later cohorts), again a positive child-driven earnings gap.
results.horizon: average earnings penalty over event times 11–20, by birth cohort
results.outcome_variable: Average earnings penalty (%)

results.why: Dynamic decomposition quantifying how much of the population-wide gender gap in earnings children create: the child-related band is about 19 percent of earnings at the end of the period, a positive child-driven earnings gap. Derivation: Child-related inequality band rises from 15.5 percent in 1980 [row 3] to about 19 percent at the end of the period [row 4], the figure counterpart of the stated increase from about 18 percent to 20 percent of the gender gap in earnings.
results.outcome_variable: Decomposition of gender inequality in earnings (%)

results.why: Same decomposition with education dummies added as controls; child-related inequality is essentially unchanged at about 18.5 percent, so it is the same quantity measured again.
results.outcome_variable: Decomposition of gender inequality in earnings (%)

claims.cause: time since the start of incarceration
claims.notes: The abstract anchor only announces that average frequency and duration across the first year are examined; the introduction supplies the direction (weekly visits stable).; The sample-wide average frequency profile that the claim is literally about is shown in Figure A-1 of the Online Supporting Material, which was not extracted; the matched estimates are the latent-class profiles of the same month-to-frequency relation in Figure 1A. Classes 4 and 5 are in rows of Figure 1A that were not printed in the extraction, so they could not be matched to a row number.

results.why: Within the largest latent class the monthly visit-frequency profile is flat from month 1 to month 12, agreeing with the claim that time since the start of incarceration leaves visit frequency unchanged; the overall sample average (Figure A-1) was not extracted, so this class-level profile is the closest extracted estimate, and the body selects the five-class model as the preferable one. Derivation: Class 1 mean visits month 12 = 0.50 (row 4) vs month 1 = 0.45 (row 1): +0.05 visits/month across the first year, i.e. essentially flat.
results.outcome_variable: # visits

results.why: This is the class-2 side of the same time-to-frequency profile and it rises steeply over the first year, contradicting the 'no effect of time on frequency' reading that holds only for the overall average; the body selects the five-class model as the preferable one. Derivation: Class 2 mean visits month 12 = 5.3 (row 9) vs month 1 = 1.1 (row 5): +4.2 visits/month over the first year (peak 6.05 at month 9, row 8).
results.outcome_variable: # visits

results.why: The class-3 frequency profile falls markedly across the first year, so this extracted estimate disagrees with the claim's 'no effect' direction; the body selects the five-class model as the preferable one. Derivation: Class 3 mean visits month 12 = 1.35 (row 13) vs month 1 = 2.4 (row 10): −1.05 visits/month over the first year (peak 3.5 at month 4, row 11).
results.outcome_variable: # visits

claims.statement: The paper provides evidence that national immigration policies produce spillover effects on migration behavior, estimated from stricter family reunification rules in Denmark.

We refer to such responses as spillover effects.

claims.notes: The abstract only compares, for workers with higher education, trade-induced moves from mid- to high-wage occupations with moves from mid- to low-wage occupations. The existence and positive direction of the mid- to low-wage move for this group is my inference from that comparison; it is nowhere stated as such. Added because the comparison claim S6 qualifies it.
claims.effect: movement from mid- to low-wage occupations

results.why: The ImpComp x College coefficient on low-wage employment (-0.864) is where the claim's higher-education population enters; the implied net move into low-wage jobs is still positive (0.575) but about half that of less-educated mid-wage workers. Derivation: ImpComp 1.439 + ImpComp x College -0.864 = 0.575 years of low-wage employment for college-educated mid-wage workers, roughly half the 1.439 of other exposed mid-wage workers.
results.subgroup: college-educated workers in mid-wage occupations as of 1999
results.outcome_variable: LOW^e_is (years of employment in low-wage occupations of worker i in period s)

results.why: High-wage side of the comparison: for college-educated mid-wage workers the trade-induced gain in high-wage employment (2.009 years) exceeds their move into low-wage jobs. Derivation: High-wage side: 0.131 + 1.878 = 2.009 years; low-wage side (Table 4 Panel A col 3): 1.439 - 0.864 = 0.575 years; 2.009 > 0.575.
results.outcome_variable: HIGH^e_is (years of employment in high-wage occupations of worker i in period s)

results.why: Low-wage side of the comparison: college education significantly cuts the trade-induced move into low-wage jobs (-0.864), leaving 0.575 years, well below the high-wage side. Derivation: Low-wage side: 1.439 + (-0.864) = 0.575 years, against 0.131 + 1.878 = 2.009 years on the high-wage side.
results.outcome_variable: LOW^e_is (years of employment in low-wage occupations of worker i in period s)

results.why: Mirror of the high-wage side for the least educated: their upward move is wiped out (about zero), confirming that moving up is a higher-education phenomenon. Derivation: 0.731 + (-0.755) = -0.024, about zero years of high-wage employment for high-school-educated mid-wage workers.
results.outcome_variable: HIGH^e_is (years of employment in high-wage occupations of worker i in period s)

results.why: Mirror of the low-wage side: the least educated move disproportionately down (+0.757 interaction), the opposite ranking to the college-educated. Derivation: 0.924 + 0.757 = 1.681 years of low-wage employment for high-school-educated mid-wage workers, versus about zero on their high-wage side.
results.outcome_variable: LOW^e_is (years of employment in low-wage occupations of worker i in period s)

claims.statement: Cancer decreases employment
claims.anchor_quote: Our main findings are the following: the negative effect of cancer on employment is stronger if the pre-cancer occupation requires high levels of manual skills or low levels of cognitive skills; the educational gradient diminishes substantially if we allow the effects of cancer to also depend on pre-cancer skill requirements; and cancer is not associated with occupational mobility, indicating potential for policies that reduce labour market frictions for cancer survivors.
claims.scope_period: fourth year after the cancer diagnosis
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, Danish administrative registers combined with O*NET skill requirement data
claims.intro_sentence: For both genders, cancer reduces the probability of being employed in the fourth year after diagnosis by about 7 percentage points, relative to the non-cancer group.
claims.magnitude_stated: about 7 percentage points
claims.scope_population: workers employed at baseline (two years before the diagnosis) who survived five years after the diagnosis
claims.scope_identification: comparison of cancer survivors with a matched control group of individuals without cancer, controlling for baseline characteristics (unconfoundedness)

results.why: Cancer x manual skills in the main Table 4 specification for males (-0.002): negatively signed as claimed but insignificant, exactly as the introduction reports.

results.why: Male manual-skill gradient with later cancer patients as controls (-0.001, insignificant).
results.outcome_variable: Employed in year t+4 (dummy)

results.outcome_variable: Full-timer in t+4 (dummy for being employed full time)

results.why: Manual-skill gradient on out-of-labour-force status for males (+0.005), same direction on the complementary margin but insignificant.
results.outcome_variable: Out of labour force in t+4 (dummy; neither employed nor unemployed)

results.why: Disability pension, a permanent exit from employment: the male manual-skill gradient is positive and significant (+0.012), which the paper invokes for this finding.

claims.statement: Measured inequality of opportunity for income is high in the United States.
claims.anchor_quote: First, with types based only on gender and parental income rank as the circumstances beyond people’s control, measured IOp for income is high in the United States and far from negligible in Denmark: before taxes and transfers, the lower-bound Gini coefficients for individual earnings and family income opportunities are in the 0.21-024 range in the United States and in the 0.08–0.12 range in Denmark.

results.why: The panel's explicit female low-minus-high education gap rows show the education gap in the probability of dying between 50 and 65 widening across successive cohorts; this is the women's side of the education indicator and the paper's main-text 50–65 cohort analysis. Derivation: Female low-minus-high education gap in probability of dying 50–65: 0.049 in the 1954 cohort (row 15) − 0.033 in the 1936 cohort (row 14) = +0.016, i.e. the gap widens by 1.6 percentage points across cohorts.
results.outcome_variable: Probability of dying between 50 and 65

results.why: Low-educated men's flat cohort trajectory against the steep decline for high-educated men gives the widening education gap for men; the gap itself is derived from the printed level rows. Derivation: Men 1954: low education 0.172 (row 9) − high education 0.062 (row 13) = 0.110; men 1936: 0.174 (row 7) − 0.110 (row 12) = 0.064; gap widens by 4.6 percentage points across cohorts.
results.outcome_variable: Probability of dying between 50 and 65

results.why: The equivalent-age restatement of the same education comparison for men, declining across cohorts, is a second expression of the widening gap. Derivation: Equivalent age of low-educated men falls from 61.2 in 1936 (row 6) to 56.9 in 1954 (row 7); measured against the age-65 high-education benchmark the gap widens from 3.8 to 8.1 years (row 11).
results.outcome_variable: Equivalent age

results.why: The equivalent-age version of the women's education comparison also widens across cohorts, supporting the same estimand. Derivation: Equivalent age of low-educated women falls from 62.4 in 1936 (row 1) to 59.2 in 1954 (row 3); against the age-65 benchmark the gap widens from 2.6 to 5.8 years (row 10).
results.outcome_variable: Equivalent age

claims.notes: The abstract anchor only announces the finding as the absence of a retirement (food) consumption puzzle; the introduction defines that puzzle as a drop in food expenditure at retirement, which supplies the effect variable and the direction being rejected.

results.why: Retirement from employment of the single main shopper on log food expenditure is insignificant (0.0244, p=0.26), the base estimate supporting 'no effect/no puzzle' for singles; the body calls this the main specification.
results.outcome_variable: Log expenditure (DKK/std.pers./month)

results.why: The alternative retirement pathway (from OLM) on single-household log food expenditure is also insignificant (−0.0275, p=0.54), agreeing with the no-effect claim.
results.subgroup: single-adult households, retiring from outside the labor market
results.outcome_variable: Log expenditure (DKK/std.pers./month)

results.why: For couples the main shopper's retirement from work raises log food expenditure significantly (0.0512, p=0.003, about 5%), so it contradicts 'no effect' while still contradicting a decline (no puzzle).

results.why: Retirement from OLM in couple households raises log food expenditure by 0.0621, marginally significant (p=0.087), a positive rather than null effect.

results.why: The spouse's retirement from work has no significant effect on household log food expenditure (−0.0044, p=0.81), a separate treatment definition supporting the no-effect claim.

results.why: The spouse's retirement from OLM is likewise insignificant for log food expenditure (−0.0316, p=0.34).

results.why: The grade-9 × early-pandemic interaction in the interaction model is the cohort's pandemic-period deviation from pre-pandemic growth; it is small and not significant, agreeing with the claim of no pandemic effect on academic self-efficacy, and the body focuses on these during-pandemic interactions as the estimates of pandemic impact. Derivation: Early pandemic [1] −0.009 + Grade level 9 # Early pandemic [28] −0.016 = −0.025 at grade 9; Early pandemic [1] −0.009 + Grade level 8 # Early pandemic [21] −0.027 = −0.036 at grade 8 (March 2020); pandemic-specific change = +0.011, i.e. negligible.

results.why: This during-pandemic interaction is significantly negative but almost entirely pre-existing cohort trend: net of the cohort's pre-pandemic grade-6 gap the extra decline is −0.006, the negligible pandemic impact the abstract claims. Derivation: Full pandemic [3] −0.078 + Grade level 9 # Full pandemic [30] −0.047 = −0.125 at grade 9; Full pandemic [3] −0.078 + Grade level 6 # Full pandemic [17] −0.041 = −0.119 at grade 6 (pre-pandemic, March 2020); additional pandemic impact = −0.006.
results.outcome_variable: Academic self-efficacy

results.why: The grade-7 during-pandemic interaction for the full-pandemic cohort is significantly negative and, net of the pre-pandemic grade-6 gap, still a −0.053 extra decline, so this horizon does not agree with a strict null pandemic effect. Derivation: Full pandemic [3] −0.078 + Grade level 7 # Full pandemic [24] −0.094 = −0.172 at grade 7 versus −0.119 at grade 6 (pre-pandemic): −0.053 extra decline during the pandemic.
results.outcome_variable: Academic self-efficacy

results.why: The grade-8 during-pandemic interaction is significantly negative, leaving a small but non-zero −0.025 pandemic-specific shortfall relative to the cohort's pre-pandemic gap. results.why: Without grade × cohort interactions the early-pandemic dummy is the cohort's average level difference pooling pre- and during-pandemic waves; it is significantly negative, i.e. the naive cohort contrast that the authors argue overstates the pandemic once trends are accounted for.

claims.statement: The paper matches the population of Danish workers to the universe of private-sector Danish firms, with product-level trade flows by origin and destination country.
claims.anchor_quote: We employ data that match the population of Danish workers to the universe of private-sector Danish firms, with product-level trade flows by origin- and destination-countries.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, matched worker-firm register data linked to firm-level customs trade data
claims.intro_sentence: Our worker-firm data cover the universe of private-sector Danish firms and the population of the Danish labor force during 1995–2006, allowing us to consistently track virtually every person in the Danish economy over time, regardless of his/her employment status or employer identity.
claims.scope_population: private-sector (manufacturing) Danish firms and the Danish labor force

claims.statement: The paper documents new stylized facts about offshoring and constructs instruments for offshoring and exporting.
claims.anchor_quote: We document new stylized facts about offshoring and instrument for offshoring and exporting.
claims.scope_setting: Danish manufacturing firms' product-level imports and exports
claims.intro_sentence: Firms concentrate their import purchases and export sales in a narrow but stable set of goods that are largely unique to each firm.
claims.scope_population: Danish manufacturing firms
claims.scope_identification: instruments built from partner-country × product transport-cost and world-wide import-demand/export-supply shocks, weighted by pre-sample sourcing patterns

results.why: This is the mobility side of the claim: the parent-to-child-in-law over spousal ratio is the direct estimate of the underlying intergenerational correlation b in Denmark, which the high r is said to explain; marital assortment itself is not a regressor here. paper_metadata.title: Taxing the Wealth of the Poor: Evidence from the Danish Old-Age Support Asset Test

results.why: The cross-sectional treated-versus-ineligible-control density gap just below the asset test threshold is the headline evidence that eligibility for the asset-tested check lowers liquid wealth. Derivation: Treated (age- and income-eligible) local peak just below the threshold 0.0225 [row 2] minus age-ineligible control 0.009 [row 5] (income-ineligible control 0.0085 [row 7]) ≈ 0.013 [row 10]: density is pushed below the threshold, i.e., eligible individuals hold less liquid wealth.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Same cross-sectional quantity measured on purely third-party-reported (default) liquid wealth, showing the bunching hump below the threshold is not an artifact of self-reported misreporting.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Age split of the same cross-sectional effect: the reduction in liquid wealth around the threshold is largest for the oldest eligible group. Derivation: 80+ peak just below the threshold 0.0283 [row 1] versus ineligible 60–64 at the same wealth level 0.0115 [row 5].
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Age split at the other end of the gradient: the effect is already present but smallest just after eligibility starts, consistent with a sluggish response. Derivation: 65–69 density at ≈DKK 75,000 of 0.019 [row 4] versus ineligible 60–64 of 0.0115 [row 5].
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Reform-based check on the same cause and outcome: liquid wealth below the threshold falls only after the asset-tested old-age check is introduced in 2003. Derivation: Post-introduction 2006–2007 density below the threshold minus pre-introduction 2001–2002 density = 0.014 [row 10] (e.g., 0.029 versus 0.014 at DKK 60,000, rows 4 and 2).
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: When the asset test threshold is raised in 2010 the wealth distribution moves with it, confirming that the asset test, not something else, holds liquid wealth down. Derivation: Post-reform 2013–2015 plateau between DKK ~70,000 and ~82,000 of 0.020 [row 8] versus pre-reform 2005–2009 density just below the old threshold of 0.0075 [row 6].
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: The cohort CDF comparison quantifies the level reduction in liquid wealth around the threshold that the cross-sectional excess mass implies, the 'sizable causal effect' the introduction refers to.
results.outcome_variable: Percentile

claims.statement: The asset test decreases liquid wealth.
claims.anchor_quote: We document strong behavioral responses to an asset test for an old-age support program in Denmark using comprehensive administrative data.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, old-age check (old-age support program) with a sharp asset test on liquid wealth
claims.intro_sentence: First, using cross-sectional analysis, we find a large impact of the asset test on the density distribution of liquid wealth with substantial excess density below the threshold for individuals satisfying the age and income criteria compared to those failing one of them.
claims.scope_population: low-income elderly aged 65 and over who satisfy the age and income criteria for the old-age check
claims.scope_identification: comparison of eligible individuals with control groups of comparable but ineligible individuals, using comprehensive administrative wealth data covering the full population

claims.effect: excess mass in the liquid asset density below the threshold

results.why: This is the treated-versus-control excess density just below the threshold that the abstract and introduction describe as the core cross-sectional finding. Derivation: Treated peak just below the threshold 0.0225 [row 2] − age-ineligible control 0.009 [row 5] ≈ 0.013 [row 10]; in the shares printed on the figure, 20.6% of the treated versus 11.6% and 11.2% of the two control groups hold 50–100% of the threshold.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: The same excess mass measured in third-party-reported default liquid wealth (bunching hump 0.0225 just below the threshold), showing the excess mass is not produced by self-reporting.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Age split of the excess mass: the hump below the threshold is largest for the oldest eligible, consistent with slow learning.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Age split at the young end of eligibility: excess mass is present but smallest, the lower end of the age gradient in bunching.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: There is no excess mass below the threshold before the asset-tested check exists and it emerges afterward, a reform-based test of the same excess-mass claim. Derivation: Excess-mass gap below the threshold, 2006–2007 minus 2001–2002 = 0.014 [row 10]; the printed shares grow from 14.4% pre-reform to 16.8% and 20.6% after.
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: The excess mass relocates when the threshold is raised, tying the excess mass specifically to the location of the asset test. Derivation: Post-reform 2013–2015 plateau of 0.020 between DKK ~70,000 and ~82,000 [row 8] versus the pre-reform density of 0.0075 just below the old threshold [row 6].
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: The within-cohort version of the same excess-mass comparison, reproducing the cross-sectional excess mass with the cohorts as their own controls. Derivation: Eligible (70–74) density just below the threshold 0.018 [row 1] versus the same cohorts when ineligible at 60–64, 0.0115 [row 2]; printed shares 18.4% versus 12.9% between 50% and 100% of the threshold.
results.outcome_variable: Density

claims.statement: The asset test increases excess mass in the liquid asset density below the threshold.
claims.anchor_quote: We show that the density distribution of the liquid assets targeted by the test exhibits large but diffuse excess mass below the threshold for the treated group relative to control groups of comparable but ineligible individuals.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, old-age check asset test on liquid assets
claims.intro_sentence: The fraction of individuals with wealth between 50 percent and 100 percent of the wealth threshold is almost twice as large for the treatment group as for the two control groups.
claims.magnitude_stated: large but diffuse excess mass below the threshold
claims.scope_population: treated group: individuals satisfying the age and income criteria (65 and over, low income)
claims.scope_identification: cross-sectional comparison of the liquid wealth density of the treated group with control groups of comparable but ineligible individuals (those just below the age threshold, aged 60–64 with low income, and those somewhat above the income threshold)

results.why: The cohort CDF comparison at the percentile corresponding to the asset test threshold is the estimate behind the abstract's '20 percent' reduction in liquid assets. Derivation: The causal effect is the horizontal distance between the two cumulative distributions at a given percentile; at the P66 line, which the figure places at liquid wealth of about DKK 95,000 [row 1] and which coincides with the asset test threshold [rows 6 and 7: treated reaches percentile 66, control 63, at the DKK 90,000 threshold], the figure's box prints −DKK 20,404 at P65, a −20.2% relative effect at P66.
results.outcome_variable: Percentile

results.why: The density version of the same cohort comparison, showing the mass shifted down from above the threshold that the percentile effect quantifies. Derivation: Eligible 70–74 density just below the threshold 0.018 [row 1] versus the same cohorts at 60–64, 0.0115 [row 2]; shares 18.4% versus 12.9%.
results.outcome_variable: Density

claims.statement: The old-age support program decreases liquid assets.
claims.anchor_quote: A cohort analysis exploiting the panel structure suggests that the program reduces liquid assets by 20 percent around the threshold.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, old-age check with a sharp asset test on liquid wealth
claims.intro_sentence: Next, conducting a cohort analysis that exploits the panel dimension of the data, we estimate the causal effect of the asset test at different percentiles of the liquid wealth distribution of the low-income elderly.
claims.magnitude_stated: 20 percent around the threshold
claims.scope_population: low-income elderly around the asset test threshold
claims.scope_identification: cohort analysis exploiting the panel structure of the data, comparing the liquid wealth distribution of the same cohorts at ages 60–64 (not yet eligible) versus ages 70–74, adjusting for nominal growth

results.why: This is the excess December cash withdrawal of the treated group just below the threshold that the introduction reports as the asset test response. Derivation: December mean minus other-months mean just below the threshold ≈ DKK 1,000 [row 11], against ≈ DKK 500 at higher and lower wealth levels [row 12].
results.horizon: December (end of the asset test year)
results.subgroup: age-eligible (65+) low-income singles with end-of-year wealth just below the threshold
results.outcome_variable: DKK

results.why: The level version of the same December spike in withdrawals, located just below the asset test threshold rather than elsewhere in the wealth distribution. Derivation: December peak just below the threshold DKK 3,950 [row 2] − other months at the same wealth level DKK 2,880 [row 9] ≈ DKK 1,070, the same gap read off the levels.
results.horizon: December (end of the asset test year)
results.subgroup: age-eligible (65+) low-income singles with end-of-year wealth just below the threshold
results.outcome_variable: DKK

results.why: Placebo on the slightly younger, ineligible control group: the December–other-months withdrawal gap is small (≈DKK 150) and not systematically larger around the threshold, so no direction is implied for the claim.
results.outcome_variable: DKK

claims.statement: The asset test increases cash withdrawals.
claims.anchor_quote: Analyzing high-frequency bank data on assets and cash withdrawals shows that the excess mass around the threshold largely reflects permanent rather than temporary responses.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, old-age check asset test; high-frequency bank data on assets and cash withdrawals linked to administrative data
claims.intro_sentence: We also find excess cash withdrawals in December for the treatment group with end-of-year wealth just below the threshold, which can explain this result.
claims.scope_population: treated group with end-of-year liquid wealth just below the asset test threshold
claims.scope_identification: comparison of monthly dynamics for treated individuals with a control group of slightly younger individuals, using high-frequency bank data

results.why: Permanent side of the comparison: the excess mass below the threshold is there in months when the asset test is not binding, so it is not end-of-year retiming. Derivation: January density just below the threshold 0.0185 [row 3] essentially coincides with the December hump 0.0185 [row 2]: virtually all of the excess mass is present outside the asset test month.
results.subgroup: permanent side: age-eligible (65+) low-income singles, months other than December
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Temporary side of the comparison: the month-to-December shift in the density is small relative to the excess mass that is present all year, so retiming explains only a minor part. Derivation: Other months density just above the threshold 0.0105 [row 6] − December 0.0085 [row 4] = 0.002, the December-specific shift, against the ≈0.0185 excess-mass hump present in every month [rows 2 and 3] and the vertical December–January gap of only 0.003 [row 8].
results.subgroup: temporary side: December retiming within the eligible group
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Temporary side measured through cash: withdrawals do rise in December below the threshold, but the amount is an order of magnitude smaller than the estimated wealth reduction; cash withdrawals are a proxy for the temporary response. Derivation: Excess December cash withdrawal just below the threshold ≈ DKK 1,000 [row 11], small next to the ≈ DKK 20,000 (20%) reduction in liquid wealth estimated around the threshold in the cohort analysis.
results.subgroup: temporary side: December cash withdrawals by the eligible group just below the threshold
results.outcome_variable: DKK

results.why: Upper-bound cash adjustment of the same temporary channel: even assuming no withdrawn cash is spent, significant excess mass below the threshold survives, so cash explains only a modest fraction. Derivation: Adding all December cash withdrawals back into liquid wealth raises the density just above the threshold only from 0.0085 [row 4] to 0.0092 [row 7], far short of the January/other-months level of 0.0105 [rows 5 and 6].
results.subgroup: temporary side: December cash withdrawals by the eligible group just below the threshold
results.outcome_variable: Density

results.why: Placebo validating the monthly design: for the ineligible control group the monthly wealth densities lie on top of each other (deviations ≈0.0008) with no bunching, so neither a permanent nor a temporary pattern is implied.
results.outcome_variable: Density

claims.relation: permanent responses > temporary responses
claims.moderator: type of behavioral response (permanent reduction in liquid wealth versus temporary end-of-year retiming and cash withdrawals)
claims.statement: Permanent responses account for more of the excess mass around the threshold than temporary responses.
claims.anchor_quote: Analyzing high-frequency bank data on assets and cash withdrawals shows that the excess mass around the threshold largely reflects permanent rather than temporary responses.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, old-age check asset test; high-frequency bank data on assets and cash withdrawals
claims.intro_sentence: For treated individuals, we find that the excess mass below the threshold of the asset test exists in all months of the year but is somewhat more pronounced in December.
claims.magnitude_stated: largely reflects permanent rather than temporary responses
claims.scope_population: treated group around the asset test threshold
claims.scope_identification: monthly dynamics of liquid wealth and cash withdrawals in bank data for treated individuals versus a control group of slightly younger individuals

results.why: The IV estimate of lagged Chinese import competition on the firm-level R&D worker share is the headline Danish estimate behind the stated 3% increase; the body calls column 2 of Table 2 the 'baseline specification'. Derivation: IV coefficient on Imp^CH_{it-1} = 0.00188 ≈ 0.002 (Table 2, col. 2), divided by the sample mean R&D worker share 0.07057 (Mean Y row) = 0.027 ≈ 3%, exactly the calculation stated in the paper's footnote 10 (0.002/0.071).
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share

results.why: Same cause, outcome and sample as the main estimate, estimated by OLS rather than IV, and reported as the positive association the IV specification then corrects for endogeneity.
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share

results.why: Robustness of the same IV estimate to a narrower definition of R&D workers that excludes technicians (Table 3, refinements).
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share - narrow definition (share of R&D workers excluding technicians)

results.why: Robustness of the same IV estimate to recalculating the R&D worker share excluding low-skilled workers.
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share excluding low skilled workers

results.why: Robustness of the same IV estimate to fixing the sale-share weights of the import competition variable at the firm's base year.
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share (main definition)

results.why: Robustness of the same IV estimate to an alternative import competition measure built on new EU member countries instead of China; the paper reports it is of similar magnitude to the baseline.
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share (main definition)

results.why: Interaction with the high-R&D-productivity dummy splits the same effect by firm type, a check reported alongside the baseline rather than the headline estimate. Derivation: Imp^CH_{it-1} 0.00184 + Imp^CH_{it-1}*HP 0.00100 = 0.00284; divided by mean Y 0.07057 = 4%, the figure the body reports for high-R&D-productivity firms.
results.outcome_variable: R&D worker share

claims.scope_setting: Danish firms (manufacturing), domestic and export markets
claims.intro_sentence: Using firm-level analysis, we find that in Denmark, a 100% increase in import competition raises firms’ share of R&D workers by 3% on average.
claims.magnitude_stated: a 100% increase in import competition raises firms’ share of R&D workers by 3% on average
claims.scope_population: firms

paper_metadata.title: Discontinuity in care: Practice closures among primary care providers and patient health care utilization

claims.notes: The abstract announces only that the transition is "smooth"; the introduction names the variable (geographic distance to the new PCP) and supplies the direction (about the same distance).

results.why: Closure X Post on distance to physician in the richest individual-fixed-effects specification, the strategy the body calls preferred; 0.47 km against a mean of 3.4 km is the 'about the same distance' the claim asserts (statistically significant but economically negligible).
results.outcome_variable: Distance to physician (km)

results.why: Same difference-in-differences estimate of closure on distance with only quarter and region dummies, identical at 0.47 km.
results.outcome_variable: Distance to physician (km)

results.why: Same estimate adding individual background characteristics, again 0.47 km, showing the small distance change is robust to controls.
results.outcome_variable: Distance to physician (km)

claims.statement: practice closure has no effect on distance to the PCP
claims.anchor_quote: Using an event study and population-level data of patients and providers in Denmark, we find that the transition between providers is smooth; among re-matched patients, there is little change in PCP care utilization at the extensive margin.
claims.scope_setting: primary care practice closures in Denmark
claims.intro_sentence: Our analyses deliver two sets of results: First, we show that PCP re-matches in our setting are smooth.
claims.scope_population: adult patients listed with a primary care practice that closes
claims.scope_identification: event study / difference-in-differences with individual fixed effects and a matched comparison group of patients whose practice closes three years later

claims.effect: PCP care utilization at the extensive margin

results.why: Closure X Post on the probability of any PCP visit in the individual-fixed-effects specification the body calls the preferred strategy: an insignificant 0.18 percentage-point change, the 'essentially no change' of the claim. Derivation: Closure X Post (x100) = 0.181 → 0.00181 on a mean outcome (x100) of 56 → 0.56, i.e. a statistically insignificant 0.3% of the quarterly probability of any PCP visit.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Same extensive-margin estimate with only quarter and region dummies, 0.0977 (x100) and insignificant.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Same estimate adding individual background characteristics, 0.0386 (x100) and insignificant.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Retirement-driven closures split of the any-PCP-visit effect, insignificant and near zero.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Same retirement split with background controls, still insignificant.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Retirement split with individual fixed effects, −0.0274 (x100) and insignificant, consistent with no extensive-margin change.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Non-retirement closures split of the any-PCP-visit effect, insignificant.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Same non-retirement split with background controls, insignificant.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Non-retirement split with individual fixed effects: 0.534 (x100) is statistically significant but under 1% of the 55.8 (x100) mean, still a minimal extensive-margin change.
results.outcome_variable: Any PCP visit

results.why: Closure effect on any PCP visit for patients in the lowest patient-density quintile, −0.007 with a confidence interval covering zero.
results.outcome_variable: Quintile of patient density

results.why: Closure effect on any PCP visit in the second density quintile, essentially zero (−0.001) with a confidence interval covering zero.
results.outcome_variable: Quintile of patient density

claims.statement: practice closure has no effect on PCP care utilization at the extensive margin

results.why: Closure X Post on total government (fee-for-service) reimbursement per quarter in the preferred individual-fixed-effects specification; since visits are unchanged the authors read this as more fee-for-service per visit, so the outcome is a proxy for the per-visit quantity. Derivation: Closure X Post (x100) = 212.9 against Mean outcome (x100) = 4405 is 4.8% of the mean quarterly government reimbursement; the stated 17% is the relative treatment effect read off the event study in Fig. 2 Panel B, which is not among the extracted results, and corresponds to the DKK 40 per quarter quoted on p. 9.

results.why: Reimbursement effect for retirement-driven closures, 223.1 (x100) and significant.
results.outcome_variable: Government reimbursement to PCP (DKK)

results.why: Same retirement split with background controls, 218.0 (x100).

results.why: Retirement split with individual fixed effects, 227.2 (x100), larger than the pooled effect.
results.outcome_variable: Government reimbursement to PCP (DKK)

results.why: Reimbursement effect for non-retirement closures, 183.6 (x100), weakly significant.

results.why: Same non-retirement split with background controls, 180.1 (x100).
results.outcome_variable: Government reimbursement to PCP (DKK)

results.why: Non-retirement split with individual fixed effects, 186.5 (x100) and significant, smaller than the retirement split.
results.outcome_variable: Government reimbursement to PCP (DKK)

results.why: Closure effect on PCP expenditure (government reimbursement) in the lowest density quintile, +0.044 with a confidence interval excluding zero.

results.outcome_variable: Quintile of patient density

results.why: Talk therapy is the stress-related health service the paper highlights as increasing: the treatment group moves from 14 DKK below to 12 DKK above the control group in the first year after outsourcing, the modest and transitory increase the introduction refers to. Derivation: Treatment-minus-control gap at T1 (+12 DKK, row 14) minus the pre-treatment gap at T-1 (-14 DKK, row 13) = +26 DKK, the 'average extra cost of 26 DKK ($4) per individual' reported in the text.
results.outcome_variable: Expenditure in DKK

results.why: GP expenditure is the second health indicator on which the paper finds a positive (first-year significant) effect; the treatment group closes and crosses the pre-treatment gap, agreeing with the claimed increase. Derivation: Treatment-minus-control gap at T3 (+10 DKK, row 11) minus the pre-treatment gap at T-1 (-48 DKK, row 10) = +58 DKK relative increase in GP expenditure.
results.outcome_variable: Expenditure in DKK

results.why: Total health insurance cost is the aggregate health-services-use indicator and it tests the claim but disagrees with it: the treatment group stays below the control group and the gap widens slightly, which is why the paper calls the health effect marginal. Derivation: Treatment-minus-control gap at T3 (-230 DKK, row 11) minus the pre-treatment gap at T-1 (-170 DKK, row 10) = -60 DKK, i.e. no relative increase.
results.outcome_variable: Expenditure in DKK

results.why: Psychologist/psychiatrist expenditure is the other stress-related indicator; it tests the claim but shows no relative increase (the paper states these series are almost completely parallel, i.e. no treatment effect). Derivation: Treatment-minus-control gap at T3 (-37 DKK, row 14) minus the pre-treatment gap at T-1 (-28 DKK, row 13) = -9 DKK, i.e. essentially parallel, no increase.
results.outcome_variable: Expenditure in DKK

paper_metadata.title: When inequality means equity: horizontal wage dispersion and the propensity to leave current employment across different organizational settings

claims.notes: The abstract only announces that there are contingencies under which horizontal wage dispersion goes with employees staying; the introduction names the contingency (large firms) and the direction, and states that the predictions are supported.

results.why: Model 3 is the authors' test of H1: the negative UWD × Log(size) interaction on the positive UWD main effect makes horizontal (unattributable) wage dispersion reduce the hazard of leaving among large-firm employees. Derivation: UWD 22.760 + UWD × Log(size) (−4.594) × 9 = −18.59, i.e. the UWD–hazard association is negative for employees of large firms; the interaction is what turns the positive main effect negative at large size.
results.outcome_variable: Transition away from 2002 employer (first-time job transition away from the employer the employee joined in 2002)

results.why: Marginal effects derived from model 3 — the formal test the authors run for H1 — showing the large-firm profile declining in UWD. Derivation: Pr(leave) at Log(Size)=9 falls from 0.517 at UWD = 0.02 (row 9) to 0.042 at UWD = 0.20 (row 12): −0.475.
results.outcome_variable: Pr(leave firm joined in 2002)

results.why: Large-firm subsample re-estimate: UWD lowers the hazard of leaving for essentially all large firms, the same finding as S1 obtained without the size interaction. Derivation: In the large-firm subsample the UWD effect is 2.651 + (−28.128 × decentralization): −14.2 at decentralization 0.60 and −21.3 at 0.85; it is positive only below ≈0.09, a range few large firms occupy.
results.outcome_variable: Transition away from 2002 employer (first-time job transition away from the employer the employee joined in 2002)

results.why: The same firm-size contingency re-estimated in the specification that adds the 2006 wage-transparency shock; the size interaction stays strongly negative. Derivation: UWD 24.903 + Log(size) × UWD (−5.072) × 9 = −20.75 for large firms in the pre-2006 baseline of the transparency-shock model.
results.outcome_variable: Transition away from 2002 employer (first-time job transition away from the employer the employee joined in 2002)

results.why: Large-firm shock specification: the UWD–hazard association remains negative across the decentralization range large firms actually occupy. Derivation: UWD 3.939 + Decentralization × UWD (−29.303) × 0.6 = −13.6 at decentralization 0.60; the large-firm UWD effect is negative for any decentralization above ≈0.13.
results.outcome_variable: Transition away from 2002 employer (first-time job transition away from the employer the employee joined in 2002)

results.why: Marginal effects of model 6: before the transparency law, large-firm employees' predicted hazard of leaving declines steadily in UWD. Derivation: The pre-2006 large-firm (decreasing solid) curve falls from 0.315 at UWD = 0.02 (row 4) to 0.149 at UWD = 0.20 (row 6).
results.outcome_variable: Pr(leave firm joined in 2002)

results.why: Gender split of the same large-firm marginal effects; the negative UWD–hazard relation holds for male employees. Derivation: Men, large firms, 2006 or before: Pr(leave) 0.32 at UWD = 0.02 (row 5) → 0.155 at UWD = 0.20 (row 6).
results.subgroup: men in large firms, 2006 or before
results.outcome_variable: Pr(leave firm joined in 2002)

results.why: Gender split of the same large-firm marginal effects; the negative UWD–hazard relation also holds for female employees. Derivation: Women, large firms, 2006 or before: Pr(leave) 0.29 at UWD = 0.02 (row 5) → 0.14 at UWD = 0.20 (row 6).
results.subgroup: women in large firms, 2006 or before
results.outcome_variable: Pr(leave firm joined in 2002)

results.why: Decentralized side of the comparison: the negative UWD × Decentralization interaction in the large-firm sample is the amplification itself, and the body states Table 4 supports H2. Derivation: Decentralized side: UWD 2.651 + UWD × Decentralization (−28.128) × 0.85 = −21.26 at decentralization 0.85, against +2.651 at decentralization 0; the decentralized-minus-centralized difference is −28.128 per unit of decentralization.

results.why: Decentralized side shown as marginal effects from model 4: the steepest decline in predicted hazard across UWD. Derivation: Decentralization = 0.85 profile falls from 0.56 at UWD = 0.02 (row 1) to 0.035 at UWD = 0.20 (row 2): −0.525.
results.outcome_variable: Pr(leave firm joined in 2002)

results.why: Centralized side shown as marginal effects from model 4: almost no reduction in the hazard as UWD rises. Derivation: Decentralization = 0.10 profile is essentially flat: 0.18 at UWD = 0.02 (row 7) → 0.175 at UWD = 0.20 (row 8): −0.005.
results.outcome_variable: Pr(leave firm joined in 2002)

results.why: The decentralization amplification re-estimated in the large-firm wage-transparency-shock model; the interaction is essentially unchanged (−29.303 vs −28.128). Derivation: UWD 3.939 + Decentralization × UWD (−29.303) × 0.85 = −20.97 in decentralized large firms, against +3.939 at decentralization 0.

results.why: Centralized benchmark in the shock model: the UWD coefficient at decentralization 0 is again positive (3.939***), i.e. no mobility reduction in centralized large firms.

results.why: Decentralized side in the model-7 marginal effects; the series is identified as the pre-2006 decentralized profile by its steep decline, matching Figure 2. results.why: The pooled binscatter slope of the listing premium in the loss domain (dl/dG-hat = -0.48) is the paper's headline "hockey stick": listing prices rise as potential nominal losses deepen.

results.why: In low-concavity municipalities the loss-domain slope is -0.48, a sharp listing-price response to mounting potential losses.
results.outcome_variable: Listing premium (percent ℓ)

results.outcome_variable: Listing premium (percent ℓ)

claims.statement: Parent consumption increases child consumption.
claims.anchor_quote: This paper identifies parents who participated in the Danish Expenditure Survey, links them to their children through population-wide Danish registries, and estimates the intergenerational elasticity of consumption in Denmark.
claims.intro_sentence: According to the main mobility estimates in this paper, the intergenerational elasticity of individual time-averaged earnings in Denmark is approximately 0.05–0.10, the elasticity of time-averaged family disposable income is approximately 0.20, and the elasticity of time-averaged (or permanent) consumption is approximately 0.35–0.40.

paper_metadata.title: The division of parental leave: Empirical evidence and policy design

claims.statement: The paper estimates parents' willingness to pay for parental leave from Danish administrative data on the division of leave and sharp variation in economic incentives created by the parental leave benefit system.
claims.anchor_quote: First, we estimate parents' willingness to pay for parental leave using Danish administrative data on the division of leave from almost 190,000 births combined with sharp variation in economic incentives created by the parental leave benefit system.
claims.intro_sentence: We estimate that, on average, households are willing to pay around 3% of household weekly earnings for an additional week of leave of fathers, while they are willing to pay around 17% for additional leave of mothers.
claims.scope_population: parents (mothers and fathers) around almost 190,000 births
claims.scope_identification: two-dimensional bunching at kinks in the household budget set created by the parental leave benefit system

claims.notes: The anchor states 'strong behavioral responses with significant bunching at kink points' and the introduction states that parents react to changes in the marginal cost of taking leave, but neither states a sign; the negative direction (a higher marginal cost of leave reduces leave taken, producing bunching just below kinks where the marginal cost rises) is my inference.

paper_metadata.title: Robots and immigration

claims.cause: share of non-Western immigrants in a municipality

results.why: First 2SLS specification of Table 4 (the paper's main results table) regressing firm robot adoption on the instrumented municipality non-Western immigrant share; its coefficient is the one the abstract/introduction's 12% is computed from. Derivation: Coefficient −0.457 on a 0–1 share: a one-percentage-point (0.01) rise implies −0.457 × 0.01 = −0.0046 ≈ −0.005 in the adoption probability; −0.005 / mean Y 0.042 ≈ −12%, exactly the figure the body reports for column 2 ('triggers a 0.005 (12%) decline').
results.outcome_variable: Robot adoption (extensive)

results.why: OLS counterpart of the main result (−0.296, a 7% decline relative to mean 0.042), reported as the uninstrumented benchmark the authors argue is upward biased.
results.outcome_variable: Robot adoption (extensive)

results.why: Same 2SLS estimand adding workforce-composition controls; the authors report it as showing the coefficient is stable.
results.outcome_variable: Robot adoption (extensive)

results.why: Fully controlled 2SLS with firm fixed effects; the body states it proceeds 'by including firm fixed effects as in column 4' for the remainder of the analysis, so it is the specification replicated in Tables 5–8 and Fig. 5, but the stated 12% comes from column 2.
results.outcome_variable: Robot adoption (extensive)

results.why: Robustness dropping firm fixed effects and using base-year firm/workforce characteristics; coefficient remains negative though only 10% significant.

results.why: Same specification with shift-share-corrected standard errors (Adão et al., 2019), confirming the negative effect.

claims.statement: The share of non-Western immigrants in a municipality decreases robot adoption by firms.
claims.anchor_quote: Using the Danish employer-employee matched dataset over the period 1995-2019, we show in a shift-share regression that a larger share of non-Western immigrants in a municipality leads to fewer robot adoptions at the firm-level.
claims.intro_sentence: By linking this information with firm-level robot data, we demonstrate that immigration and robotization are substitutes: a higher local share of migrant workers leads firms to adopt fewer robots.
claims.magnitude_stated: a one percentage point increase in the share of non-Western migrants decreases the probability of robot adoption by 12%
claims.scope_population: firms in the Danish employer-employee matched dataset
claims.scope_identification: shift-share instrumental variable regression exploiting exogenous immigration (1993 country-of-origin shares, Refugee Spatial Dispersal Policy)

claims.notes: The abstract anchor announces only that prime age makes immigrant workers 'particularly substitutable for robots'; the introduction sentence on separate regressions for subsets of the immigrant population names prime age as a characteristic making them substitutable, and the introduction's substitution statement supplies the negative direction.

results.why: The only regression whose treatment is the prime-age (25–55) non-Western immigrant share, instrumented with predicted working-age immigration; its significant negative coefficient is the basis for the prime-age claim.
results.subgroup: non-Western immigrants of core working age (25–55)
results.regressor: Non-West Immigrant Share (only working age pop.)
results.row_label: Non-West Immigrant Share (only working age pop.)

claims.scope_population: firms in the Danish employer-employee matched dataset; subsets of the non-Western immigrant population
claims.scope_identification: shift-share instrumental variable regressions run separately for subsets of the immigrant population

paper_metadata.title: Social Positions and Fairness Views on Inequality

claims.notes: Data/method sentence of the abstract, listed so it is not silently dropped; no cause-effect relation.
claims.statement: The paper links survey data on perceived income positions and fairness views to administrative records on reference groups, income histories, and life events.
claims.anchor_quote: We link survey data on Danish people’s perceived income positions and fairness views on inequality within various reference groups to administrative records on their reference groups, income histories, and life events.
claims.intro_sentence: To overcome these challenges, we leverage a unique dataset that we constructed by linking responses from a custom survey of a large sample of people in Denmark to detailed administrative data on their full income histories, life events, and true positions in the income distributions of different reference groups.
claims.scope_population: Danish survey respondents aged 45–50
claims.scope_identification: custom survey linked to administrative register records

claims.notes: Descriptive fact about accuracy of perceptions; no cause-effect pair.
claims.statement: People are on average well-informed about the income levels of their reference groups.
claims.anchor_quote: People are, on average, well-informed about the income levels of their reference groups.
claims.intro_sentence: On average, people perceive the overall income level (the median, which we call P50) of their reference groups correctly and, therefore, are well aware of core income differences across different groups of people.
claims.scope_population: Danish survey respondents aged 45–50
claims.scope_identification: survey perceptions compared with administrative income records

claims.cause: own income rank in the reference group
claims.effect: overestimation of own position in the reference group

results.why: The binned perceived-vs-actual cohort scatter crosses the 45-degree line at actual position ~48, i.e. overestimation below and underestimation above, so own cohort rank reduces overestimation.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position

results.why: Same quantity shown as misperception: the cohort curve starts at +20.8 percentiles of overestimation at the bottom and declines (crossing zero at ~49) as own cohort rank rises.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived - actual position within reference group

results.why: Robustness split by precision of own-income reporting: even respondents who report their own income precisely show median perceived position 24.5 at actual position ~18, so the rank gradient in overestimation is not an artefact of own-income error.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position

results.why: The 'This year' curve again shows perceived position ~20 for respondents at actual cohort position 0-3 (overestimation) rising to 85 at position 100 (underestimation).
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position this year

results.why: Within the sector reference group, low-ranked respondents strongly overestimate and the gap falls with own rank; this is the number the introduction quotes. Derivation: Sector curve at actual within-sector position 20 = 41 perceived, i.e. 'well above the 40th percentile'; overestimation = 41 − 20 = 21 percentiles at the bottom, shrinking and turning negative above the 45-degree crossing at ~50.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position within reference group

results.why: Same gradient in the municipality reference group, with the magnitude the introduction states. Derivation: Municipality curve at actual within-municipality position 20 = 30 perceived; overestimation = 30 − 20 = 10 percentiles, declining to underestimation above the ~55 crossing.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position within reference group

results.why: Misperception of position in the education group is +22.3 percentiles at the bottom of the cohort distribution and falls to zero at cohort position ~55 and below zero thereafter.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived - actual position within reference group

results.why: Misperception within the gender group is +21.6 at the bottom and crosses zero at cohort position ~47.5, so higher own rank lowers overestimation.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived - actual position within reference group

results.why: Among co-workers in the same firm the lowest-ranked bin overestimates its position by about 30-36 percentiles, and the bias shrinks and turns negative as own rank rises.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position within co-workers

results.why: The other side of the same gradient in the same panel: respondents in the top bin underestimate their position among co-workers.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position within co-workers

results.why: Among neighbours the bottom bin overestimates its rank by about 21-26 percentiles while the top bin underestimates, so own rank reduces overestimation.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position within neighbors

results.why: Among former schoolmates the lowest actual-rank bin reports a perceived position of about 28-31, far above its actual rank, with the gap vanishing and reversing at higher ranks.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position within schoolmates

claims.statement: Own income rank in a reference group decreases overestimation of own position in that group.
claims.anchor_quote: Yet, lower-ranked respondents in all groups tend to overestimate their own position among others because they believe others’ incomes are lower than they actually are, whereas the opposite holds true for higher-ranked respondents.
claims.intro_sentence: Within all reference groups, people in the upper part of the distribution believe they are ranked lower than they really are, while people in the lower part of the distribution believe they are ranked higher.
claims.scope_population: Danish survey respondents aged 45–50, all reference groups
claims.scope_identification: perceived rank compared with true rank from administrative records

results.why: The centre-bias mechanism: the slope of perceived cohort P50 on own (demeaned) income is about 0.14, so lower-income respondents perceive others' incomes as lower, which is what makes them overestimate their own rank; the cause and effect are each measured by a proxy half of the mechanism.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived P50 in reference group demeaned within group (1000 DKK)

results.why: Same mechanism in the sector reference group, where the slope of perceived P50 on own income is steepest (~0.25), matching the larger position overestimation found for sectors.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived P50 in reference group demeaned within group (1000 DKK)

results.why: The same income-driven misperception of others holds for the P95 of the group (average slope ~0.5), so low-income respondents also underestimate the top of others' distribution and place themselves higher.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived P95 in reference group demeaned within group (1000 DKK)

results.why: Rules out the rival channel: respondents who report their own income precisely still overestimate their position (24.5 perceived at actual ~18), so the overestimation must come from misperceiving others' incomes.
results.outcome_variable: Perceived position

claims.statement: home prices increase the likelihood of giving birth
claims.anchor_quote: Using rich population register data among women aged 20-44 who own a home, we find that for each 100,000 DKK increase in home prices (equivalent to $12,000), the likelihood of giving birth increases by 0.27 percentage points or 2.32%.
claims.intro_sentence: Our findings suggest that there is a positive effect of home price increases on fertility: a 100,000 DK (approximately $12,000 in 2006, adjusting for purchasing power parity) increase in home prices in the prior year increases the likelihood of giving birth by 0.27 percentage points, or 2.32% relative to the mean.
claims.magnitude_stated: for each 100,000 DKK increase in home prices (equivalent to $12,000), the likelihood of giving birth increases by 0.27 percentage points or 2.32%
claims.scope_population: women aged 20-44 who own a home
claims.scope_identification: one-year changes in home values among women who became homeowners between 1993 and 2004, following Lovenheim and Mumford (2013)

claims.notes: Only the Denmark side of the comparison is estimated in this paper; the US side (2.11% per $12,000, Lovenheim and Mumford 2013) is an external literature figure with no corresponding extracted regression column.

results.why: This is the Denmark side of the comparison: the preferred estimate whose 2.32% per $12,000 is set against the US 2.11%; the US side is a cited external estimate, not an extracted regression of this paper. Derivation: 0.0027 ÷ mean fertility rate 0.1166 = 2.32% per 100,000 DKK ≈ $12,000 PPP, compared with the US figure of 2.11% per $12,000 from Lovenheim and Mumford (2013).
results.outcome_variable: Birth (0/1) – indicator for whether the woman gave birth in year t

claims.intro_sentence: They find an effect of 2.11% for each $12,000 of home price increase, which is very close to the 2.32% effect we document in Denmark.
claims.magnitude_stated: the 2.32% effect we document in Denmark versus an effect of 2.11% for each $12,000 of home price increase in the US

paper_metadata.title: Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?

claims.notes: Abstract announces only 'little evidence of negative effects on firms'; the introduction names the outcome (total labor inputs) and states the null.

results.why: Firm total hours relative to baseline, the paper's measure of total labor inputs, scaled per 1% of the workforce on leave; the body calls the percent-of-workforce specification preferred for outcomes measured relative to baseline. Derivation: Lower 95% CI bound from the preferred column 3 estimate: −0.0479 − 1.96 × 0.0713 = −0.188 ≈ −0.19% when 1% of the workforce goes on leave.

results.why: Unconstrained side for labor costs: no detectable effect on the leave-excluded wage bill in the overall sample.

results.why: Unconstrained side for output: the overall-sample sales effect is slightly positive and tightly bounded.

results.why: Constrained side for firm survival: an increase in shutdown at no replacement firms. Derivation: Contrast in the survival proxy per 1% of the workforce on leave: no replacement firms −0.000783 versus all firms +0.000213 (table 7, col. 3), a difference of −0.000996.

results.why: Unconstrained side for firm survival: a near-zero, tightly bounded effect in the overall sample.

paper_metadata.title: Migration for co‐residence among long‐distance couples: The role of local family ties and gender

claims.notes: The finding rests on the descriptive moving patterns of Table 3 (average female share 54.2%; median distance moved 89.7 km for women vs 84.4 km for men), and Table 3 was not extracted. None of the extracted regression columns contains a regressor for being the female partner — gender is built into the outcome definition (the woman's share), so the claim is carried only by a mean/constant, not by any identifiable coefficient row.
claims.effect: share in the total distance moved
claims.statement: Being the female partner increases one's share in the total distance moved.
claims.anchor_quote: Our findings indicate that women tend to bridge the larger share of the distance when moving into co-residence.
claims.scope_period: 2009-2017 (entry into co-residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017)
claims.intro_sentence: We use data from the Danish population register on all opposite-sex couples who entered co-residence between 1 January 2009 and 31 December 2017 and who lived 60 km apart or more within Denmark before co-residence
claims.scope_population: opposite-sex long-distance couples (partners living 60 km or more apart before co-residence), aged 18-70
claims.scope_identification: cross-classified multi-level regression on Danish population register data

claims.effect: share in the total distance moved

results.why: A non-resident minor child living nearby lowers the woman's own share of the distance by 0.113; the body calls model 2 one of the two main models and notes its superior goodness-of-fit.
results.outcome_variable: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co-residence

results.why: A non-resident minor child living nearby lowers the man's own share by 0.133, the individual-level estimate for men in the same main model.
results.outcome_variable: Man's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co-residence

results.why: Having only adult non-resident children nearby lowers the woman's share by a small 0.019, a different (adult rather than minor child) definition of the tie.
results.outcome_variable: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co-residence

results.why: Having only adult non-resident children nearby moves the man's share by −0.005, negative in sign but statistically and substantively negligible.
results.outcome_variable: Man's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co-residence

results.why: Couple-level specification: when only the woman has a non-resident child living nearby her share falls by 0.062.
results.outcome_variable: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co-residence

results.why: When only the man has a non-resident child nearby the woman's share rises by 0.086, i.e. his own share falls by the same amount.
results.outcome_variable: Woman's share in the total distance moved by both partners at the start of co-residence

paper_metadata.title: Identifying behavioral responses to tax reforms: New insights and a new approach

claims.statement: The standard estimation strategy for identifying behavioral responses to income tax reforms relies on an assumption of constant trend differentials across the income distribution.
claims.anchor_quote: Cast in the context of income taxation, we show that, in essence, the standard estimation strategy relies on an assumption that any time differences in income across the income distribution remain constant in the absence of tax reforms.
claims.intro_sentence: Cast in the context of income taxation, we show that, in essence, the standard estimation strategy relies on an assumption that any time differences in income across the income distribution remain constant in the absence of tax reforms.

claims.statement: The assumption of constant trend differentials underlying the standard estimation strategy can be validated econometrically and graphically by non-parametrically comparing trend differentials in a reform period and a pre-reform period.
claims.anchor_quote: The assumption of constant trend differentials is equivalent to the common trend assumption underlying DiD studies, and we show how the assumption can be validated econometrically and graphically, in a way similar to the comparison of pre-trends in DiD studies.
claims.intro_sentence: Hence, we can validate the identifying assumption by non-parametrically comparing trend differentials in two periods: a reform period, where a reform changes tax rates differently for different groups, and a pre-reform period, where ideally the tax system was stable.
