paper_metadata.title: An Empirical Model of Wage Dispersion with Sorting

claims.statement: The paper estimates an equilibrium on-the-job search model with endogenous search intensity.
claims.anchor_quote: We estimate an equilibrium on-the-job search model with endogenous search intensity.
claims.scope_identification: structural estimation of an equilibrium on-the-job search model

claims.statement: The model is estimated on Danish matched employer-employee data.
claims.anchor_quote: The model is estimated on Danish-matched employer–employee data.
claims.intro_sentence: Using Danish matched employer–employee data we find evidence of positive sorting in the labour market.
claims.scope_population: Danish workers and firms in matched employer-employee data

claims.statement: Firms are ranked by revealed preference using the fraction of hires poached from other firms, the poaching rank.
claims.anchor_quote: Firms are ranked through revealed preference by the fraction of hires that is poached from other firms: the poaching rank.
claims.intro_sentence: Firm-type rank is identified by revealed preference based on the fraction of a firm's hires that comes directly from other firms as opposed to from unemployment: the poaching index.
claims.scope_identification: revealed preference firm ranking (poaching index)

claims.statement: Identification is obtained from firm rank conditional mobility and wage patterns.
claims.anchor_quote: Identification is obtained by firm rank conditional mobility and wage patterns.
claims.intro_sentence: With this, identification is obtained through firm rank conditional mobility and wage patterns.
claims.scope_identification: firm rank conditional mobility and wage patterns

claims.notes: The abstract anchor announces sorting as a source of wage variation; the introduction names the two variables and gives the positive direction (positive sorting, correlation 0.39).

results.why: The positive covariance between the worker-skill component h* and the firm-productivity component p* of simulated wages is the estimated model's direct statement that more skilled workers are matched with more productive firms; the body treats the estimated 'Sorting economy' as the benchmark against the no-sorting counterfactual. Derivation: Sorting 0.033 = Productivity, 2Cov(h*,p*) 0.008 (24%) + Bargaining, 2Cov(h*,E[q*|p*,h*]) 0.025 (76%, the stated three-quarters); the productivity-sorting quarter is the printed 0.008 / 24%.
results.outcome_variable: ln w (log of simulated wages w = w(h,p,q) from the estimated model); the decomposition is of Var(ln w*), the variance of predicted log wages ln w* = ξ0 + h* + p* + q*

results.why: Descriptive data counterpart: the poaching-rank CDF for <12 years of schooling lies above that for >12 years by up to 0.19 (0.33 vs 0.17 at rank 0.2), so more educated (higher-skill) workers are matched with higher-ranked, more productive firms.
results.outcome_variable: CDF

results.why: Measured through AKM worker and firm wage fixed effects in the Danish data, the sorting covariance is −0.002 (−2% of wage variance), contradicting the claimed positive skill–productivity association, which the authors attribute to bias in the AKM proxy.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log hourly wage of worker i in panel observation n)

results.why: The same AKM wage-sorting statistic on data simulated from the estimated model is +0.007 (6%), near zero, showing the positively-sorted estimated economy reproduces the near-zero AKM sorting of the data.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log wage of worker i in panel observation n, simulated from the estimated structural model)

results.why: Worker wage effects are less dispersed within a firm than in the population, which the paper states is an implication of positive sorting of worker types to firm types. Derivation: E[Var(χi|J(i)=j)] = 0.051 < Var(χi) = 0.069 (row 0), the implication of sorting stated in Section 7.2.1.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log hourly wage of worker i in panel observation n)

results.why: The estimated model reproduces the pattern in simulated data: E[Var(χi|J(i)=j)] = 0.051 below Var(χi) = 0.054.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log wage of worker i in panel observation n, simulated from the estimated structural model)

results.why: Conditioning on the firm wage fixed effect instead of firm identity, E[Var(χi|φJ(i))] = 0.065 is nearly the unconditional 0.069, i.e. almost no sorting detected in the wage-fixed-effect lens.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log hourly wage of worker i in panel observation n)

results.why: Same check in simulated data: E[Var(χi|φJ(i))] = 0.053 versus Var(χi) = 0.054, so the wage-fixed-effect lens detects almost no sorting even though the model's true corr(h,p) is 0.39.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log wage of worker i in panel observation n, simulated from the estimated structural model)

claims.statement: worker skill increases firm productivity of the employer a worker is matched with
claims.anchor_quote: Wage variation is decomposed into four sources: sorting (40%), worker heterogeneity (32%), firm heterogeneity (18%), and frictional competition (10%).
claims.intro_sentence: Using Danish matched employer–employee data we find evidence of positive sorting in the labour market.
claims.magnitude_stated: a correlation between worker skill and firm productivity of 0.39
claims.scope_population: Danish workers and firms in matched employer-employee data
claims.scope_identification: estimated equilibrium on-the-job search model with firm ranking by poaching index

claims.notes: The abstract anchor assigns sorting a 40% share of the decomposition; the introduction states the direction explicitly as a contribution to wage dispersion.

results.why: The sorting component of the structural decomposition of Var(ln w*) in the estimated ('Sorting') economy is 0.033, 40% of predicted log-wage variance — the printed estimate behind the stated 40%.
results.outcome_variable: ln w (log of simulated wages w = w(h,p,q) from the estimated model); the decomposition is of Var(ln w*), the variance of predicted log wages ln w* = ξ0 + h* + p* + q*

results.why: The counterfactual economy with sorting shut down has lower predicted log-wage variance, but its search intensities are calibrated to hold the structural Var(ln w) = 0.100 fixed, so the drop cannot be read as sorting's effect on total wage variation. Derivation: Total Var(ln w*) = 0.082 (Sorting economy) versus 0.047 (No sorting economy).
results.outcome_variable: ln w (log of simulated wages from the counterfactual no-sorting economy); the decomposition is of Var(ln w*), the variance of predicted log wages ln w* = ξ0 + h* + p* + q*

results.why: Measured through the AKM decomposition of the same Danish wages, sorting accounts for −2% (−0.002) of log-wage variance, so in that lens sorting does not raise wage variation — the contrast the paper draws with its own 40%.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log hourly wage of worker i in panel observation n)

results.why: AKM applied to data simulated from the estimated, positively sorted model yields a wage-sorting contribution of only 0.007 (6%), showing the AKM share badly understates the structural sorting contribution.
results.outcome_variable: ln w_in (log wage of worker i in panel observation n, simulated from the estimated structural model)

results.why: Largest direct effect (0.60) is in the lowest maternal-earnings quartile; inequality is not measured directly but read off the gradient in subgroup direct effects.
Second-quartile direct effect (0.572) lies on the declining income gradient the inequality claim rests on.
Third-quartile direct effect (0.508) continues the monotone decline in the direct effect with family income.

Smallest direct effect (0.421) in the top earnings quartile: the high-income side of the gradient that makes the direct effect inequality-reducing. Derivation: Direct effect gap low- minus high-income = 0.600 (quartile 1) − 0.421 (quartile 4) = 0.179, the equalising gradient behind the claim.
Direct effect for low-educated mothers (0.572) is the high end of the education gradient cited as evidence of reduced inequality.
Intermediate education subgroup (0.531) sits between the basic and further education effects, on the declining gradient.

Smallest direct effect (0.39) for highly educated mothers: the high-SES side of the education gradient that makes the direct effect inequality-reducing. Derivation: Direct effect gap low- minus high-education = 0.572 (basic) − 0.390 (further) = 0.182, the equalising education gradient.

claims.statement: Influenza vaccination increases the rate of dementia
claims.anchor_quote: Vaccination during follow-up was associated with a slightly higher rate of dementia when adjusted for sociodemographic factors and comorbidities, both within and after the first 5 years from first vaccination (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.04; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03–1.05).
claims.intro_sentence: This nationwide registry-based study investigated whether late-life influenza vaccination, including the number and timing of vaccinations, is associated with a reduced risk of dementia.
claims.magnitude_stated: incidence rate ratio [IRR] 1.04; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.03–1.05
claims.scope_population: dementia-free adults aged ≥65 years without previous influenza vaccinations
claims.scope_identification: register-based cohort study; Poisson regression adjusted for sociodemographic factors and comorbidities; estimated both within and after the first 5 years from first vaccination

results.why: Endpoint coefficient of the fully adjusted dose-response gradient that the abstract's decreasing-with-number statement rests on. Derivation: Fully adjusted dementia IRRs fall monotonically across vaccination counts: 1.14 (row 2, one), 1.08 (row 3, two), 1.02 (row 4, three–five), 0.95 (row 5, ≥6); the ≥6 row is the end point of that gradient.

results.why: Full-sample estimate of crowd-out of reform-induced total pension contributions into financial-asset savings; a coefficient above −1 implies total savings rose, the quantity the abstract's claim refers to. Derivation: Pass-through to total savings = 1 + α2 = 1 + (−0.650) = 0.35 of the pension-contribution increase; the estimate is insignificant and the 95% CI [−1.362, 0.063] is wide, so full crowd-out is not ruled out in the full sample.
results.outcome_variable: S (savings in financial assets relative to total gross payments)

results.why: This is the precise estimate the body relies on for the total-savings conclusion (it 'rules out crowd-out in excess of 22%'), but it covers the extraordinary-contributor subgroup, so it is a separate estimand from column (3); the body does not use the words preferred/baseline/main for it. Derivation: Pass-through = 1 + α2 = 1 + (−0.086) = 0.91; the CI lower bound −0.222 bounds crowd-out at 22%, i.e. at least 78% of the contribution increase passes through to total savings.
results.outcome_variable: S (savings in financial assets relative to total gross payments)

results.why: Tests the other margin of offset: higher employer pension contributions crowd IN private pension contributions (+0.156) rather than crowding them out, supporting the net increase in total savings.

results.why: Same no-offset check within pension accounts for the extraordinary-contributor subgroup: still positive crowd-in (0.050), so the contribution increase is not funded by cutting other pension saving.

results.why: The estimated negative dependence of schooling measurement error on true schooling is the cause, and through eq. (3) it implies the 38% IV amplification the abstract states; the body calls col. 4 the general model and Table A4 labels it the baseline. Derivation: ρ_s = −.276 (row 14, Table 2 col. 4) enters the IV bias formula E(β̂_IV) = β/(1+ρ_s): 1/(1 − 0.276) = 1.381, i.e. the IV bias factor of 1.381 printed at the foot of Table 2 col. 4 and the stated 38% overestimation of the true returns to schooling.

Derivation: Reminder letter 0.087 ÷ below-cut-off age-3 adherence of non-adherent children ≈ 0.19 ("Around 19% of untreated non-adherent children (below the cut-off) catch up with the schedule and reach adherence at age 3", p. 8; Table 2 below-cut-off mean 0.19) = 0.46 ≈ 50%.
results.horizon: adherence at age 3 (one year after the letter)
results.outcome_variable: All vacs. at age 3 (indicator for full adherence at age 3)

results.why: The specification curve re-estimates the same age-3 adherence discontinuity in the non-adherent sample across 56 bandwidth/estimator choices, with the main specification at 0.088, so it is a robustness check on the same estimand.

results.outcome_variable: (unlabeled)

results.why: Same RD design and main specification but scaled to an entire cohort: the policy raises full adherence at age 3 by 2.6 percentage points, a distinct population from the non-adherent sample.

results.outcome_variable: All vacs. at age 3 (indicator for full adherence at age 3)

results.why: Specification curve for the full population sample; the main-specification point (0.025) reproduces Table 3 column (2) and all 95% CIs exclude zero.

results.why: A count rather than an adherence indicator, so a separate quantity: the policy raises vaccinations in the third year by 0.115 (a 43% increase), confirming the adherence effect with a related measure.

results.outcome_variable: No. vacs., year 3 — the number of vaccinations received during year 3 (the year after treatment)

results.why: Tests whether the adherence effect extends to a later vaccination round; the point estimate 0.015 (s.e. 0.017) is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the paper reads it as no spill-over, so the direction cannot be told.
results.horizon: booster MMR participation by age 5 (later vaccination round)
results.outcome_variable: Booster MMR, age 5 — indicator for participation in the booster MMR vaccination by age 5

results.why: Discontinuity in completion of the DiTeKiPolHib sequence at age 3 (0.88 − 0.872 ≈ 1 percentage point, from 87% to 88% in the text), the pertussis side of the herd-immunity statement.

results.why: Reluctance side of the comparison: the complement of the same discontinuity gives the 72.1% non-responsive (reluctant) share, which the paper contrasts with the 8.7% responsive share. claims.intro_sentence: We first show that inflation backcasts predict inflation forecast errors, and conversely that inflation forecasts predict inflation backcast errors. This shows that memory is imperfect, and that errors in forecasts are linked to imperfect recall.
claims.scope_population: Danish consumer expectations survey respondents (households)
claims.scope_identification: affect-cued recall tests, including comparisons of regressions with and without inflation backcasts as a covariate

paper_metadata.title: Undeclared Danish Labor: Using the Labor Input Method with Linked Individual-Level Tax Data to Estimate Undeclared Work in Denmark

claims.notes: Methodological contribution presented as a finding; no cause-effect pair with a direction.
claims.statement: An individual-level approach has advantages over the standard approach when estimating undeclared work with the labor input method.
claims.anchor_quote: This paper shows the advantages of an individual-level approach when estimating undeclared work using the labor input method.
claims.intro_sentence: This paper shows the advantages of an individual-level approach when estimating undeclared work using the labor input method.
claims.scope_identification: labor input method applied to Danish Labor Force Survey data linked at the individual level with administrative tax (eIndkomst) data

claims.notes: Descriptive methodological finding about the aggregated approach; no directional cause-effect pair stated.
claims.statement: An aggregated labor input approach has shortcomings: it assumes all workers with missing administrative data work fully undeclared, cannot adequately account for overtime or extreme values, and cannot detect and correct errors in administrative data.
claims.anchor_quote: It shows the shortcomings of an aggregated approach, namely assuming that all workers with missing administrative data are working fully undeclared, being unable to adequately account for overtime, extreme values and not being able to detect and correct for errors in the administrative data.
claims.intro_sentence: Using Denmark as a case study, this paper uses individual-level linked data to show the potential shortcomings of applying the labor input method with an aggregated dataset.
claims.scope_identification: labor input method with aggregated versus individual-level linked survey and administrative data

claims.notes: Methodological result presented as a finding; no directional cause-effect pair.
claims.statement: The shortcomings of the aggregated approach can be overcome to a large extent by using an individual-level linked dataset, yielding results useful for researchers and tax authorities.
claims.anchor_quote: The paper illustrates how these shortcomings can be overcome to a large extent by using an individual-level linked dataset and yield results that are useful both for researchers and for tax authorities.
claims.intro_sentence: The study shows that using individual-level linked data can adequately overcome problems of misinterpreting missing data in aggregated data, not being able to account for legitimate overtime, extreme values and correcting for measurement error in the administrative data.
claims.scope_identification: labor input method with individual-level linked Labor Force Survey and administrative tax data

claims.notes: A capability of the method / a quantity it can estimate; no cause-effect relation stated.
claims.statement: The individual-level labor input method can estimate undeclared work for the self-employed.
claims.anchor_quote: It shows that the method can estimate undeclared work for the self-employed, as well as show seasonal and industry differences in undeclared labor.
claims.intro_sentence: Using individual-level linked data can provide estimates for the self-employed and of industry sector differences and seasonal patterns in undeclared work, which are useful for both researchers and tax authorities.
claims.scope_population: self-employed
claims.scope_identification: labor input method with individual-level linked Labor Force Survey and administrative tax data

claims.notes: Announces that differences can be shown; the abstract states no direction for any concrete pair of variables.
claims.statement: The individual-level labor input method can show seasonal and industry differences in undeclared labor.
claims.anchor_quote: It shows that the method can estimate undeclared work for the self-employed, as well as show seasonal and industry differences in undeclared labor.
claims.intro_sentence: Using individual-level linked data can provide estimates for the self-employed and of industry sector differences and seasonal patterns in undeclared work, which are useful for both researchers and tax authorities.
claims.scope_identification: labor input method with individual-level linked Labor Force Survey and administrative tax data

claims.notes: Data/method contribution presented as a result of the paper; no cause-effect relation.
claims.statement: Using Denmark as a case study, the paper provides detailed instruction for applying the individual-level approach in other countries with Labor Force Survey data.
claims.anchor_quote: Denmark is used as a case study, and unlike other papers utilizing individual-level data, this paper provides detailed instruction for how a similar approach can be applied in other countries with Labor Force Survey data.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark (case study); other Labor Force Survey countries
claims.intro_sentence: Unlike other papers utilizing the labor input method, the paper provides detailed guidance for how to use individual-level data, thereby encouraging the application of the approach in other countries with Labor Force Survey (LFS) data.

paper_metadata.title: Pension reform and wealth inequality: Theory and evidence

claims.notes: The anchor alone states cause, effect and direction ("transform ... into asset owners").

results.why: This is the theory figure's FF savings level for the low-β agents: under the mandate they hold the full mandated asset position, whereas without it they hold almost nothing — exactly the claim that mandated FF plans turn low savers into asset owners. Derivation: FF total savings for all β below β^F are flat at the mandate, 0.57 of the plotted range [row 1], against 0.05 for the same agents under laissez faire [row 3] and ~0.02 under PAYG [row 4].
results.outcome_variable: Total savings

results.why: The PAYG counterpart in the same panel — private savings of low-β agents are essentially zero (they sit at the zero-saving corner), the baseline against which the FF mandate creates asset ownership.
results.outcome_variable: Total savings

results.why: Quantitative counterpart of the theoretical claim in the calibrated Danish model: the move to mandated FF pensions raises the asset holdings of the most impatient (low-saving) agents the most. Derivation: Peak assets of the most impatient type rise from 125 thousand 2015 DKK in 1992 [F10::A row 7] to 780 in 2017 [row 7], a 6.2-fold increase; relative to the most patient type the gap falls from 1820/125 ≈ 14.6 to 3490/780 ≈ 4.5 ("almost 15 times" vs "about five times" in the text).
results.outcome_variable: thousands of 2015 DKK

results.why: Shows that for the least patient agents essentially all accumulated assets are the mandated pension assets, i.e. the mandate itself is what makes them asset owners; the portfolio share is a proxy for the asset-ownership outcome. Derivation: Pension share of total assets for β = 0.9189 rises from 0.93 in 1992 [row 8] to 1.00 in 2017 [row 1].
results.outcome_variable: share

claims.statement: Mandated fully-funded pension plans increase asset ownership
claims.anchor_quote: Mandated fully-funded plans transform individuals with lower incomes, often characterized as low savers, into asset owners, and may also imply a more equal wealth distribution than pay-as-you-go-based systems.
claims.scope_setting: simple two-period life-cycle model of pension systems
claims.intro_sentence: By contrast, in a FF scheme, the explicit saving mandate converts low income, possibly hand-to-mouth people, into savers; consequently, total retirement saving increases.
claims.scope_population: individuals with lower incomes, often characterized as low savers
claims.scope_identification: theoretical life-cycle (overlapping-generations) model

claims.notes: Stated relative to pay-as-you-go-based systems ("a more equal wealth distribution than pay-as-you-go-based systems"); the abstract hedges with "may".

results.why: The theory Lorenz panel: the cumulated wealth share held by the low-β (poorest) agents is highest under the mandated FF scheme, which is the model's statement that FF implies a more equal wealth distribution than PAYG. Derivation: At β = β^P the FF Lorenz curve lies at 0.17 of total wealth [row 1] against 0.09 under laissez faire [row 2] and ~0.02 under PAYG [row 3]: the FF curve is closer to the 45-degree line at the bottom of the distribution.
results.subgroup: all agents in the two-period model (read at the PAYG cutoff β^P)
results.outcome_variable: Cumultative wealth, % of total wealth

results.why: The PAYG side of the same Lorenz comparison — the bottom of the distribution holds essentially nothing under PAYG, the benchmark the claim compares the mandated FF scheme to.
results.subgroup: all agents in the two-period model (read at the PAYG cutoff β^P)
results.outcome_variable: Cumultative wealth, % of total wealth

claims.statement: Mandated fully-funded pension plans decrease wealth inequality
claims.anchor_quote: Mandated fully-funded plans transform individuals with lower incomes, often characterized as low savers, into asset owners, and may also imply a more equal wealth distribution than pay-as-you-go-based systems.
claims.scope_setting: simple two-period life-cycle model of pension systems; comparison with pay-as-you-go-based systems
claims.intro_sentence: Therefore, a transition from a PAYG system to a multi-pillar structure has the potential to decrease wealth inequality.
claims.scope_identification: theoretical life-cycle (overlapping-generations) model

claims.notes: Descriptive fact about the setting, documented by the paper; no cause-effect relation stated.
claims.statement: Denmark witnessed declining wealth inequality over the last decades
claims.anchor_quote: To test the empirical validity of these predictions, the paper explores a pension reform in Denmark, a country that witnessed declining wealth inequality over the last decades.
claims.intro_sentence: First, unlike most other advanced economies, Denmark has experienced a downward trend in wealth inequality over the last decades.
claims.scope_population: Danish households
claims.scope_identification: descriptive register-data evidence

claims.notes: The anchor alone states cause, effect and direction ("a key factor explaining the downward trend in wealth inequality").

results.why: The calibrated model, whose only policy change between 1992 and 2017 is the pension reform, delivers the fall in the 60-69 Gini on which the paper's headline attribution rests; the body calls this the baseline model against which the no-reform counterfactuals are run. Derivation: Model Gini for the 60-69 group 0.626 in 1992 [row 1] − 0.537 in 2017 [row 7] = −0.089, i.e. the "decline of almost ten percentage points" and the −8.9 pp full (baseline) model change in Table 4 row (a).
results.outcome_variable: (unlabeled axis; Gini coefficient)

results.why: The empirical decline the model is asked to reproduce; calendar time spanning the reform stands in for the reform itself, so it documents rather than identifies the effect. Derivation: Data Gini for 60-69 falls from 0.626 in 1992 [row 2] to 0.512 in 2017 [row 8], −0.114, matching the −18% change in Table 1.
results.outcome_variable: (unlabeled axis; Gini coefficient)

results.why: On the broader wealth measure that adds imputed PAYG wealth, inequality among the near-retired rises rather than falls, so this check runs against the claim's direction. Derivation: Extended-wealth Gini for heads 60-69 rises from about 0.17 in 1986 [row 6] and 0.19 around 1992 [row 7] to 0.225 in 2017 [row 9]; Table 7 reports 0.19 to 0.23, +17.5%.
results.subgroup: households with head aged 60-69, extended wealth (net wealth + imputed PAYG wealth)
results.outcome_variable: Gini coefficient

results.why: Same calibrated baseline model for the whole population: the modelled pension transition produces a falling wealth Gini over 1992-2017 (the model in fact slightly overpredicts the empirical decline). Derivation: Model full-population Gini 0.772 in 1992 [row 9] → 0.68 in 2010 [row 14]; with Table 3's model value of 0.642 for 2017, 0.772 − 0.642 = −0.130, the −13.0 pp full (baseline) model change in Table 4 row (a).
results.outcome_variable: (unlabeled axis; Gini coefficient)

results.why: Lorenz-curve version of the same finding, which model and data share: the share held by the lowest deciles rises over the reform period, so the distribution becomes more equal. Derivation: Cumulative wealth share of the bottom decile in the data rises from −0.055 in 1992 [row 1] to −0.035 in 2017 [row 11].
results.outcome_variable: cumulative wealth share

results.why: Wealth dispersion across types collapses over the modelled transition because the mandated pension lifts the impatient agents' assets most — the mechanism behind the modelled fall in the Gini. Derivation: Ratio of peak assets of the most patient to the most impatient type falls from 1820/125 ≈ 14.6 in 1992 [F10::A rows 1 and 7] to 3490/780 ≈ 4.5 in 2017 [rows 1 and 7].
results.subgroup: full population of simulated β types (dispersion across types)
results.outcome_variable: thousands of 2015 DKK

results.why: Including imputed PAYG wealth leaves the all-household Gini essentially flat (if anything higher), i.e. the measured decline disappears on the broader wealth concept — a check that contradicts the claim's direction. Derivation: HP-trend extended-wealth Gini for all households is 0.65 at the start of the sample [row 1], peaks near 0.825 around 2000 [row 4] and is 0.755 in 2017 [row 5]; Table 7 reports 0.75 in both 1992 and 2017 (+0.67%).
results.subgroup: all households, extended wealth (net wealth + imputed PAYG wealth)
results.outcome_variable: Gini coefficient

results.why: Even on the extended wealth measure the poorest two deciles became relatively richer, which the paper reads as support for the mechanism through which the reform lowered inequality at the bottom. Derivation: The 2017 extended-wealth Lorenz curve lies about 0.04 above the 1992 curve at deciles 2-3 [row 5] (−0.08 [row 4] vs −0.12 [row 1]).
results.subgroup: full population, bottom two deciles, extended wealth
results.outcome_variable: Cumulative wealth share

results.why: The motivating empirical trend the paper sets out to explain: the wealth Gini declines over exactly the decades of the pension transition, with calendar time standing in for the reform. Derivation: HP-trend Gini falls from 0.744 in 1986 [row 1] to 0.707 in 2017 [row 6], a total decline of 0.037 [row 7]; Table 1 reports 0.75 to 0.69, −8%.
results.outcome_variable: Gini coefficient

results.why: The share-based counterpart of the Gini decline in the same figure, and precisely the margin the theory predicts the FF transition acts on (the wealth of low savers). Derivation: Bottom-50% HP-trend wealth share rises from 1.05% in 1986 [row 1] to 2.9% in 2017 [row 4], +1.85 pp [row 5], while the top-10% share falls about 2 pp from its early-1990s peak [row 10].
results.outcome_variable: LEFT axis: 'Wealth share, bottom 50%'; RIGHT axis: 'Wealth share, top 10%'

results.why: Shows the rise in the bottom-50% share is driven by the lowest deciles, the households the reform forced into pension saving — the distributional margin the claim runs through. Derivation: Share of net wealth held by decile 1 rises from −3.8% in 1986 [row 1] (minimum −6.9% in 1991 [row 3]) to −2.2% in 2017 [row 9].
results.subgroup: all Danish households, lowest wealth decile
results.outcome_variable: Share (%) of net wealth

results.why: Cross-sectional decomposition showing that the funded pension assets built up by the reform are what lift the bottom of the 2017 wealth distribution, i.e. lower measured inequality once they are counted. Derivation: Cumulated net wealth share of the first decile is −3.5% including pension assets [row 1] against −8% excluding them [row 9]; the including-pension Lorenz curve lies above the excluding-pension curve at every decile.
results.horizon: 2017 cross-section (wealth with vs without pension assets)
results.outcome_variable: Cumulated net wealth share

paper_metadata.title: Summaries of Articles
Gender gaps in the effects of childhood family environment: Do they persist into adulthood?

claims.notes: The design estimates only male–female differences: every printed coefficient is the male dummy or a Male × family-environment interaction. The family-environment main effects (the level effect for girls, and hence for boys) are controlled for but never reported, so no extracted column contains an estimate of the effect of family environment on boys' grade-school outcomes alone. The differential is mapped under S3.

claims.anchor_quote: Our results are consistent with U.S. findings that boys benefit more from an advantageous family environment than do girls in terms of grade-school outcomes.

paper_metadata.title: Can Women Have Children and a Career? IV Evidence from IVF Treatments

claims.statement: The paper introduces a new IV strategy based on IVF-induced fertility variation among childless women to estimate the causal effect of having children on their career.
claims.anchor_quote: This paper introduces a new IV strategy based on IVF (in vitro fertilization) induced fertility variation among childless women to estimate the causal effect of having children on their career.
claims.intro_sentence: In particular, we sample childless women who go through IVF, treat IVF treatment success at the first IVF treatment as a natural experiment, and subsequently compare the working careers of women after a successful first treatment (treatment group) to those of women after a failed first treatment (comparison group).
claims.scope_population: childless women entering their first IVF treatment
claims.scope_identification: instrumental variables using success at the first IVF treatment as instrument for childbearing

claims.cause: information reporting for charitable tax deductions

results.why: Figure 1a is the headline pre/post series: the jump of ~148,000 claims between the last self-reporting year (2007) and the first information-reporting year (2008) is the doubling stated in the abstract. Derivation: number of claims 2008 (row 6) 300,000 ÷ number 2007 (row 5) 152,000 = 1.97, i.e. the stated doubling; equivalently the jump of 148,000 claims printed in row 10 (text: 150,311 in 2007 vs 300,122 in 2008).
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: Second reading of the same Figure 1a panel: the 2008 level of 299,000 claims against 152,000 in 2007 reproduces the same pre/post doubling. Derivation: number 2008 (row 12) 299,000 ÷ number 2007 (row 11) 152,000 = 1.97, a doubling.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: Figure 1b splits the rise by claim size; the smallest-claim bin jumps roughly ten-fold at the reform, the dominant component of the overall increase. Derivation: 0-500 bin 2008 (row 3) 81,000 ÷ 0-500 bin 2007 (row 2) 7,500 ≈ 10.8, the 'almost 10-fold increase' in claims below DKK500.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: Same small-claim surge on the sample that drops trained accountants, showing the ten-fold rise is not an artefact of that group. Derivation: 0-500 bin 2008 (row 3) 80,000 ÷ 0-500 bin 2007 (row 2) 8,000 = 10.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: The finer 2008 claim-size distribution shows a mass of very small claims that is absent from the otherwise near-identical 2006 and 2007 distributions. Derivation: 2008 leftmost bar 33,000 (this panel, row 1) against the 2007 panel's sub-DKK500 bar height of about 1,500 (dk_W2781798209::F2::2007, row 3).
results.outcome_variable: No.

results.why: The DKK501-1,500 bin also more than doubles at the reform, the second-largest component of the overall rise in the number of claims. Derivation: 501-1,500 bin 2008 (row 9) 71,000 ÷ 501-1,500 bin 2007 (row 8) 31,500 = 2.25, the 'more than doubling' described in the text.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: Same DKK501-1,500 doubling when trained accountants are excluded from the population. Derivation: 501-1,500 bin 2008 (row 8) 71,000 ÷ 501-1,500 bin 2007 (row 7) 30,000 = 2.37.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: Among accountants the number of small claims also jumps at the reform, so the extensive-margin rise in claims is present even in this high-knowledge subgroup. Derivation: 0-500 bin 2008 (row 3) 130 ÷ 0-500 bin 2007 (row 2) 56 = 2.3.
results.outcome_variable: Number

claims.statement: Information reporting for charitable tax deductions increases the number of deductions claimed
claims.anchor_quote: We show that the introduction of information reporting for charitable tax deductions in Denmark in 2008 was associated with a doubling in the number of deductions claimed, and a 15% rise in the total value of claims, which can be credibly attributed to previously unclaimed deductions.
claims.intro_sentence: Contrary to expectations, the introduction of information reporting for charitable deduction in Denmark was associated with an immediate doubling in the number of taxpayers claiming a charitable deduction; there was also a 15% rise in the total value of deductions claimed.
claims.magnitude_stated: a doubling in the number of deductions claimed
claims.scope_population: taxpayers claiming charitable deductions
claims.scope_identification: pre/post comparison around the 2008 policy change

claims.cause: information reporting for charitable tax deductions

results.why: Figure 1a is the only extracted exhibit bearing on the value of claims; the stated 15% rise is the product of the plotted number of claims and the plotted average claim value before and after 2008 (the regression estimate in equation (2) was not extracted). Derivation: Total value = number × average value: 2008 number (row 6) 300,122 × mean DKK2,697 = DKK809m, versus 2007 number (row 5) 150,311 × mean DKK4,671 (row 15 average value 2007 ≈ 4,700) = DKK702m; 809/702 = 1.153, the stated 15% rise.
results.outcome_variable: Number

claims.statement: Information reporting for charitable tax deductions increases the total value of claims
claims.anchor_quote: We show that the introduction of information reporting for charitable tax deductions in Denmark in 2008 was associated with a doubling in the number of deductions claimed, and a 15% rise in the total value of claims, which can be credibly attributed to previously unclaimed deductions.
claims.intro_sentence: We show that the surge in the number of deductions claimed can be credibly attributed to unclaimed deductions under the prior self-reporting regime.
claims.magnitude_stated: a 15% rise in the total value of claims
claims.scope_population: taxpayers claiming charitable deductions
claims.scope_identification: pre/post comparison around the 2008 policy change

claims.statement: Evasion is not the main source of non-compliance for charitable tax deductions; overclaiming under the self-reporting regime was negligible
claims.anchor_quote: This contradicts the presumption that evasion is the main source of non-compliance for deductions, and that the use of information reporting raises revenue collections.
claims.intro_sentence: Using data from a pre-reform large-scale randomized audit experiment in Denmark, we document that there was negligible overclaiming of charitable tax deductions under the self-reporting regime.
claims.scope_population: taxpayers
claims.scope_identification: pre-reform large-scale randomized audit experiment

claims.cause: information reporting for charitable tax deductions
claims.notes: The abstract anchor only denies the presumption that information reporting raises revenue; the introduction supplies the direction (a net loss in revenue).

results.why: No extracted result has revenue as an outcome; the revenue loss is the mechanical tax-expenditure counterpart of the rise in deductions claimed shown in Figure 1a, so the outcome is a proxy. Derivation: Deductions claimed rose from 150,311 × DKK4,671 = DKK702m in 2007 (row 5, row 15) to 300,122 × DKK2,697 = DKK809m in 2008 (row 6), i.e. about DKK49 million more deductions (text p.899); at the one-third subsidy rate this is roughly DKK16 million of forgone revenue per year.
results.outcome_variable: Number

claims.statement: Information reporting for charitable tax deductions decreases revenue collections
claims.anchor_quote: This contradicts the presumption that evasion is the main source of non-compliance for deductions, and that the use of information reporting raises revenue collections.
claims.intro_sentence: For charitable deductions in Denmark, the net effect of introducing information reporting was a loss in revenue.
claims.scope_population: charitable deductions
claims.scope_identification: pre/post comparison around the 2008 policy change

results.why: Having another self-reported deduction proxies a lower marginal compliance cost of filing one more deduction; the 8.4pp higher probability of self-reporting a charitable deduction in 2007 is consistent with compliance cost suppressing self-reporting.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, and zero otherwise)

results.why: Same fixed-cost test with a different self-reported deduction type: taxpayers with a childminders/fisherman deduction are 8.2pp more likely to have self-reported a charitable deduction.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, and zero otherwise)

results.why: Third self-reported deduction type: a 12.9pp higher self-reporting probability, again consistent with a fixed compliance cost deterring claiming.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, and zero otherwise)

results.why: The transport deduction is pre-populated but, as the paper notes, frequently adjusted by taxpayers and so effectively self-reported; its 18.5pp coefficient is read as further compliance-cost evidence (the genuinely pre-populated unemployment-insurance and alimony rows do not measure the cause and are not matched).
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, and zero otherwise)

results.why: Accountant status holds information and salience frictions fixed, so the rise in small accountant claims at the reform is attributed to record-keeping cost suppressing self-reporting of low-value deductions. Derivation: 0-500 bin 2008 (row 3) 130 against 2007 (row 2) 56, roughly a 2.3-fold rise.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: For claims above DKK500 accountants show no reform break, so compliance cost does not explain the bulk of the missing deductions — the test disagrees with the unqualified claim, which the paper itself qualifies to 'only a small share'. Derivation: 1,501-3,000 bin: 172 (2006, row 11), 197 (2007, row 12), 228 (2008, row 13), 265 (2009), 303 (2010) — a smooth trend with no break at the reform.
results.outcome_variable: Number

results.why: The comparison side of the accountant test: the large jump in mid-sized claims among non-accountants, absent for accountants with the same assumed record-keeping costs, cannot be due to compliance cost and must reflect other frictions. Derivation: 1,501-3,000 bin 2008 (row 13) 89,000 against 2007 (row 12) 56,500, a 57% jump, versus no break for accountants in dk_W2781798209::F6::b.
results.subgroup: all taxpayers less accountants, claims of DKK1,501-3,000
results.outcome_variable: Number

claims.anchor_quote: Various tests suggest that compliance cost, passive choice and overwithholding suppressed self-reporting of deductions.
claims.intro_sentence: We also provide evidence that record-keeping costs can explain only a small share of the missing charitable deductions.
claims.scope_population: taxpayers
claims.scope_identification: various tests using the 2008 reform

results.why: Saving 2% above the firm-occupation pension default proxies active (non-passive) choice; it raises the probability of self-reporting a charitable deduction in 2007 by 1.9pp, i.e. passivity suppresses self-reporting.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, zero otherwise)

results.why: Same active-saving indicator in the combined regression on the common sample, which the paper uses to show the effect is independent of the other activity proxies.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, zero otherwise)

results.why: Opening a non-employer capital pension account is the second proxy for active choice (top-bracket sample only); it raises self-reporting probability by 1.2pp.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, zero otherwise)

results.why: Same capital-pension indicator in the combined common-sample regression; still positive (0.007) though no longer statistically significant.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, zero otherwise)

results.why: Amending one's default withholding is the paper's second proxy for active rather than passive behaviour; such taxpayers are 8.5pp more likely to have self-reported an eligible charitable deduction.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, zero otherwise)

results.why: Same withholding-change indicator in the combined regression (6.5pp), confirming an independent effect alongside the retirement-saving proxies.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, zero otherwise)

claims.statement: Passive choice decreases self-reporting of deductions
claims.anchor_quote: Various tests suggest that compliance cost, passive choice and overwithholding suppressed self-reporting of deductions.
claims.intro_sentence: Using a range of tests, we provide evidence that awareness of incentives, loss aversion and default behaviour were drivers of reporting behaviour under the self-reporting regime.
claims.scope_population: taxpayers
claims.scope_identification: various tests using the 2008 reform

results.why: A small preliminary surplus is overwithholding (tax withheld exceeds liability); the printed confidence interval [-0.074, -0.064] shows the coefficient is -0.069, so overwithheld taxpayers are 6.9pp less likely to self-report a charitable deduction — the graphical counterpart (Fig. 4b) was not extracted.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, and zero otherwise)

results.why: The mirror-image measure: taxpayers who were under-withheld and owe a small amount are 2.8pp more likely to self-report, agreeing with the claim that overwithholding (a refund position) suppresses self-reporting.
results.outcome_variable: Reported a Charitable Deduction in 2007 (indicator taking the value unity if the taxpayer reported a charitable deduction in 2007, and zero otherwise)

results.why: Cumulative share of injured workers who participated in a higher degree within ten years of the accident, the stock counterpart of the Figure 1 flow response. results.why: Same enrollment outcome, split by degree physicality; a smaller 3.9 percent of injured workers enroll in degrees of similar physical intensity.

results.subgroup: degrees targeting occupations of higher physical intensity

results.why: Operationalises the abstract's 'degrees that build on their past training and experience': 8.5 of the 14 percent enroll within their own career cluster.
results.subgroup: degrees in the same career cluster as the original job

results.why: Complementary split of the same enrollment response: 5.1 percent enroll outside their original career cluster.
results.subgroup: degrees in a different career cluster

results.why: Age split of the post-injury higher-degree enrollment: 38.7 percent of injured workers in their twenties take up higher education.

results.why: Split by the nature of the accident: permanent loss of earning ability produces a 13.4 percent enrollment rate, the margin that carries the claim.

claims.notes: Method/data presented as a contribution in the abstract; no cause-effect relation.
claims.statement: Using administrative data for the population of Danish men and women, the paper develops an empirical model of the joint earnings dynamics of siblings and youth community peers.

results.subgroup: GPA, post-diagnosis income controlled (pecuniary channel netted out)
results.outcome_variable: Coefficient estimates

results.why: Total-effect side of the comparison for GPA (-0.040), the benchmark against which the income-controlled estimate is read.
results.outcome_variable: Coefficient estimates

results.why: Pecuniary side of the comparison for completing secondary education: almost unchanged by controlling for income. Derivation: Completion effect with post-diagnosis income controlled (this row) = -0.012 (1.2%) versus -0.013 (1.3%) without it (Fig. 1 panel C, row 1): a 0.001 difference, so the pecuniary channel explains under a tenth of the completion effect.
results.outcome_variable: Coefficient estimates

results.why: Total-effect side of the comparison for completion (-0.013), the benchmark for the income-controlled estimate.

claims.relation: driven by non-pecuniary costs rather than pecuniary costs
claims.moderator: cost pathway (non-pecuniary versus pecuniary)
claims.statement: the effects of a parental health shock on children's school achievements are driven more by non-pecuniary costs than by pecuniary costs
claims.anchor_quote: The effects appear to be driven by non-pecuniary costs rather than pecuniary costs.
claims.intro_sentence: Second, we investigate the pecuniary pathway on the average effect of a parental cancer diagnosis by including average family income three years after the diagnosis (the year prior to the diagnosis) as a control variable.
claims.scope_population: Danish children with a parent diagnosed with cancer
claims.scope_identification: coarsened exact matching of children with parental cancer to children with no parental health shock, combined with OLS

claims.notes: The survivor-only prognosis gradient is reported only in Fig. 2(a) (and Supplementary Tables A9-A10); no Fig. 2 panel appears among the extracted figure panels, so no estimate restricted to children whose diagnosed parent survived is available to match.
claims.statement: size of the health shock decreases school performance
claims.anchor_quote: Moreover, we find that the negative effects on school performance increase in the size of the health shock for both survivors and non-survivors.
claims.intro_sentence: Fourth, little attention has been given to understand the consequences of non-fatal health shocks. In this study we are able to measure the impact of health shocks amongst parental survivors and thus able to disentangle morbidity and mortality effects.
claims.scope_population: Danish children whose cancer-diagnosed parent survived
claims.scope_identification: coarsened exact matching; size of the health shock measured by cancer specific survival rates

claims.notes: The non-survivor (parental cancer death) prognosis gradient is reported only in Fig. 2(b) (and Supplementary Tables A9-A10); that figure's panels were not extracted, so there is nothing to match.
claims.statement: size of the health shock decreases school performance
claims.anchor_quote: Moreover, we find that the negative effects on school performance increase in the size of the health shock for both survivors and non-survivors.
claims.intro_sentence: Third, we contribute to the literature by minimising endogeneity problems related to mortality outcomes.
claims.scope_population: Danish children whose cancer-diagnosed parent died
claims.scope_identification: coarsened exact matching; size of the health shock measured by cancer specific survival rates

paper_metadata.title: The Moving Parts of Life: A Meso-level Analysis of Interregional Migration Patterns after Life Course Events

claims.statement: The paper constructs event group-specific origin–destination interregional migration flow matrices for non-overlapping life course events from Danish household register data.
claims.anchor_quote: While interregional migration flow data related to life-events are generally not publicly available from statistical offices, we present a way to construct origin–destination migration flow matrices from Danish register data on migration, economic and social events at the household level.
claims.intro_sentence: One of our unique contributions is that of building a novel data set that constructs event group-specific interregional migration flow matrices, where event groups are non-overlapping.
claims.scope_population: full population of Danish residents grouped into eight non-overlapping life course event groups
claims.scope_identification: construction of event group-specific origin–destination flow matrices from population register data

paper_metadata.title: The Temporality of Being NEET: A Longitudinal Study of NEET Occurrences among Young Adults in Denmark

claims.notes: The abstract anchor states the share of NEET-labelled young adults who cannot be characterized as at risk; the introduction supplies the explicit direction ('being NEET does not express a risk of social exclusion as such').

results.why: Largest cluster (71.1%): only ~12% are NEET at the end of the nine-year window, so for the bulk of the labelled-NEET population the status is brief and seasonal rather than a trajectory of exclusion — the estimate carrying the 'four out of five' claim. Derivation: Cluster A n = 11,593 (71.1% of 16,314) + cluster B n = 1,327 (8.1%) = 12,920/16,314 = 79.2%, i.e. 'four out of five'; cluster A's combined NEET share stays at 0.07-0.12 across the window.
results.subgroup: cluster A (few, short NEET occurrences; 71.1% of study population)

results.why: Second side of the 'four out of five' group: the NEET peak at ages 19-20 is transitory, with only ~17% NEET at the end of the window, so being NEET here does not signal exclusion risk. Derivation: Cluster B n = 1,327 (8.1%) added to cluster A's 71.1% gives 79.2% of 16,314 = four out of five; cluster B's NEET share peaks at 0.60 around month 50 but falls back to 0.17 by month 107.
results.subgroup: cluster B (one long initial NEET occurrence around ages 19-20; 8.1% of study population)

results.why: Individual-level sequence plot of the same cluster: ~90% of panel area is non-NEET (education/employment), confirming at the individual level that NEET occurrences here are short and scattered.
results.subgroup: cluster A (few, short NEET occurrences; 71.1% of study population)

results.why: Same cluster shown as individual sequences: ~80% of the panel is non-NEET and the green NEET block is a bounded episode (months ~42-60), supporting the reading that this NEET spell is a gap year, not exclusion.
results.subgroup: cluster B (one long initial NEET occurrence around ages 19-20; 8.1% of study population)

results.why: The counter-side within the same analysis: for this 7.4%, the NEET share plateaus at ~0.85 from month 60 onwards, i.e. being NEET here does coincide with long-term exclusion, contrary to the claim's blanket direction.
results.subgroup: cluster C (early-onset, long-term first NEET episode; 7.4% of study population)

results.why: Individual sequences for the same cluster: ~75% of rows are still in NEET01 at month 100, confirming the persistent exclusion pattern for this minority.
results.subgroup: cluster C (early-onset, long-term first NEET episode; 7.4% of study population)

results.why: For this 4.9%, NEET peaks at 0.78 and ~45% are still NEET at the end of the window, a long-term pattern the paper itself reads as risk of exclusion — the fifth of the population the claim excepts.
results.subgroup: cluster D (short first NEET episode developing into a long second episode; 4.9% of study population)
results.outcome_variable: Freq. (n=797)

results.why: Same cluster at the individual level: ~60% of rows are in the long second NEET episode at month 100, supporting the persistent-exclusion reading.
results.subgroup: cluster D (short first NEET episode developing into a long second episode; 4.9% of study population)

results.why: For this 3.8%, repeated NEET occurrences become long-lasting, with ~55% still NEET at month 107 — a trajectory the paper treats as precarious, i.e. against the claim's direction for this subgroup.
results.subgroup: cluster E (several NEET occurrences gradually becoming long-lasting; 3.8% of study population)
results.outcome_variable: Freq. (n=621)

results.why: Individual sequences for the same cluster: ~50% of rows are in a long-lasting NEET state at month 105, supporting the gradual-entrenchment reading.
results.subgroup: cluster E (several NEET occurrences gradually becoming long-lasting; 3.8% of study population)

results.why: For this 4.7%, churning between NEET and other activities ends with ~72% NEET at month 107, the precarious pattern the paper contrasts with the four-fifths who are not at risk.
results.subgroup: cluster F (churning, up to 12 transitions, NEETPLUS; 4.7% of study population)
results.outcome_variable: Freq. (n=762)

results.why: Same cluster at the individual level: ~55% of rows are in NEETPLUS at month 108 after a fragmented middle period, supporting the precarious-churning reading.
results.subgroup: cluster F (churning, up to 12 transitions, NEETPLUS; 4.7% of study population)

results.outcome_variable: (unlabeled axis)

results.why: Fifth URE decile: prediction from median liquid wealth stays within about 5 percentage points of the full estimate. Derivation: Interpolated from median liquid wealth = 0.665 versus actual 0.71 (row 13): prediction error 0.045.
results.outcome_variable: (unlabeled axis)

claims.notes: The abstract anchor only announces that frictions affect labor market outcomes; the introduction names the outcome (sharp bunching at the kink point) and the direction (no sign of sharp bunching; frictions prevent its formation).

results.why: The density read off at the kink point itself is lower than the smooth pre-reform mode located below it, i.e. no sharp excess mass at the kink, which the paper reads as evidence of optimization frictions. Derivation: Pre-reform density at the kink (excess income = 0) = 6.8 [row 5] is below the 2008 peak density of 7.7 [row 1], which sits at excess income −5 [row 2]: no spike at the kink point.
results.subgroup: students taking up less than full benefits, pre-reform (2006-2008)
results.outcome_variable: Density (%)

paper_metadata.title: Employer-to-Employer Transitions and Time Aggregation Bias

claims.cause: defining EE transitions based on quarterly data

results.why: The figure panel plots EE rates under the adjacent-quarter definition against the daily benchmark, and row [13] is the quarterly-minus-daily gap that is exactly the overestimate the claim asserts (the headline 5.45 vs 3.75 appears in the text and in Table 2, which was not extracted). Derivation: Row [13] quarterly(adjacent)−daily gap = 1.9 pp in 2008, i.e. row [1] 6.7% minus row [3] 4.8%; 1.9/6.7 = 28%, the same object as the stated sample-average overestimate (5.45−3.75)/5.45 ≈ 30%.
results.outcome_variable: Employer-to-Employer rate

results.why: Same quarterly-minus-daily gap read at the 2010 trough (1.4 pp), showing the adjacent-quarter definition overstates the EE rate throughout the series, not only at the start.
results.outcome_variable: Employer-to-Employer rate

claims.statement: Defining EE transitions based on quarterly data increases the measured EE transition rate.
claims.anchor_quote: Defining EE transitions based on quarterly data overestimates the EE transition rate by approximately 30% compared to daily data.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, administrative matched employer-employee data (BFL) with exact daily start and end dates of employment spells
claims.intro_sentence: The main result of this paper is that time aggregation bias overestimates the EE transition rate by up to 30%.
claims.magnitude_stated: by approximately 30% compared to daily data
claims.scope_population: all persons in Denmark having a job from age 18 to 60
claims.scope_identification: comparison of EE transition rates computed from daily employment-spell data with rates computed after aggregating the same spells to quarterly frequency (adjacent-quarter definition)

claims.effect: time aggregation bias in the EE transition rate

results.why: Baseline regression without a trend of the quarterly-to-daily differential EE rate on the unemployment gap; the negative coefficient means the bias shrinks when unemployment rises (recession), and the body cites it as Column (1). Derivation: Cyclical indicator −0.090 (row [0]) × 2 pp = −0.18 pp; relative to the mean differential quarterly rate of 1.67 pp (Table 1, Mean Dep. Var.) this is 10.8% ≈ the stated 11%.
results.outcome_variable: Differential quarterly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from quarterly to daily frequency

results.why: Same regression adding a linear time trend ('Including a time trend leads to the same conclusion, see Column (2)'), so it is a check on the same estimand.
results.outcome_variable: Differential quarterly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from quarterly to daily frequency

results.why: The monthly-frequency counterpart of the cyclicality regression; the body singles this column out ('For EE at the monthly frequency, the difference is 0.065 percentage points using the model with a time trend'), but the abstract and introduction do not.
results.outcome_variable: Differential monthly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from monthly to daily frequency

results.why: Same monthly-to-daily cyclicality estimate without the time trend (−0.063), the specification the authors report alongside the cited one.
results.outcome_variable: Differential monthly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from monthly to daily frequency

results.why: Same regression with the change in the unemployment rate as cyclical indicator — a different treatment definition, hence its own estimand; as printed the coefficient is positive (+0.052), i.e. a deteriorating labour market raises rather than lowers the bias, although the text claims it confirms the procyclicality result.
results.outcome_variable: Differential quarterly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from quarterly to daily frequency

results.why: Same change-in-unemployment specification with a linear time trend (+0.090), again printed with the opposite sign to the claimed direction.
results.outcome_variable: Differential quarterly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from quarterly to daily frequency

results.why: Monthly-to-daily differential on the change in unemployment, no trend; printed coefficient +0.018 goes the opposite way to 'bias reduced in recessions' (and is small relative to its standard error).
results.outcome_variable: Differential monthly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from monthly to daily frequency

results.why: Same monthly change-in-unemployment estimate with a time trend (+0.042); a check on the same estimand, also printed with the sign opposite to the claim.
results.outcome_variable: Differential monthly EE transition rate: percentage point difference in the employer-to-employer transition rate from monthly to daily frequency

results.why: Mechanism evidence the introduction invokes: the recession/expansion CDF ratio at 90 days is 0.979 < 1, so fewer non-employment spells end within a quarter in recessions, leaving less scope for misclassification — a proxy outcome for the bias itself.
results.outcome_variable: CDF EE Recession / CDF EE Expansion

results.why: The plotted quarterly-minus-daily gap narrows at the 2010 recession trough relative to the 2008 expansion, the graphical counterpart of the regression result. Derivation: Row [14] gap at the 2010 recession trough = 1.4 pp vs row [13] gap in the 2008 expansion = 1.9 pp.
results.outcome_variable: Employer-to-Employer rate

claims.statement: Recessions decrease the time aggregation bias in the EE transition rate.
claims.anchor_quote: The bias is procyclical and is reduced by more than 10% in recessions.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, administrative matched employer-employee data (BFL) with daily employment spell information
claims.intro_sentence: Next, we show that misclassification is procyclical.
claims.magnitude_stated: reduced by more than 10% in recessions; increasing the unemployment rate by two percentage points decreases the difference between the quarterly EE and daily EE rates by 11%
claims.scope_population: all persons in Denmark having a job from age 18 to 60
claims.scope_identification: regression of the quarterly-to-daily (and monthly-to-daily) differential EE transition rate on a cyclical indicator (deviation of unemployment from its HP-filtered trend), with and without a linear time trend

claims.statement: The paper proposes an algorithm that uses earnings, and not just start and end dates of jobs, to redefine EE transitions.
claims.anchor_quote: We propose an algorithm that uses earnings and not just start and end dates of jobs to redefine EE transitions.
claims.scope_setting: Denmark, quarterly-frequency information constructed from Danish matched employer-employee data
claims.intro_sentence: The algorithm uses workers' earnings before and after job mobility, and not just start and end dates of jobs, to redefine EE transitions.

claims.notes: The abstract anchor only announces that the proposed definition 'performs better'; the introduction names the outcome (EE rate accuracy) and the direction (significantly improves).
claims.effect: accuracy of the measured EE transition rate

results.why: This is the extracted exhibit in which the algorithm's earnings thresholds (the cause) map into the measured quarterly EE rate, and raising the thresholds lowers the rate toward the daily truth, i.e. improves accuracy as claimed. Derivation: Row [1] (no reclassification, x=y=0) EE rate 8.5% → row [2] (maximal reclassification, x=y=100) EE rate 5.3%, i.e. applying the earnings thresholds moves the quarterly EE rate toward the true daily benchmark (3.75% in the paper's text; Table 2 reports 4.22% / 3.75% corrected vs 5.44% uncorrected, but Table 2 was not extracted).
